cia-0000119204:
From about November 1987, this CIA document reports a sighting of a possible burial site for missing Americans in Xieng Khouang Province, Laos. The province, home to the Plain of Jars, saw heavy fighting and bombing during the war. Reports of graves were among the grimmest leads the agency followed.

Each reported site had to be checked against records of lost aircraft and missing crews. Most leads led nowhere, but each one mattered to a family waiting for news. The document preserves the sighting as it was reported, a single entry in the huge file of the missing that stayed open long after the war ended.
cia-0000119704: A January 1953 CIA paper surveys conditions and trends in the Middle East that bear on American security. Oil, the new state of Israel, and rising Arab national feeling were combining into a lasting problem for Washington. The paper maps those pressures at the start of a stormy decade. Papers of this breadth set the frame for smaller country studies, giving leaders one map of a region that would occupy them for years.
cia-0000124304: An October 1972 CIA document covers air raid shelters at Luta, Shenyang, and Shih-chia-chuang, plus the Peking subway and suspected sites, the heading breaking off. China's civil defense building was read in Washington as a sign of fear of war. The paper maps the shelters as plotted. Shelter digging on that scale suggested a state preparing its people for attack, and analysts weighed it as evidence in judging how real China's war fears were.
cia-0000132504: Cuban reaction to anti-Castro invasions fills a CIA document dated February 3, 1961. The word invasions sits in quotation marks in the headline, showing the agency's care with the term. The great invasion was still two months off, but smaller raids had already begun. The short document gauges how Havana answered those early attacks and prepared its people for larger ones to come.
cia-0000132604:
A blunt verdict stands as the headline of a CIA paper dated August 6, 1960: the Cuban situation worsens. By that summer Washington had stopped hoping that a moderate Cuba would emerge from the revolution. Seizures of property, the Soviet embrace, and the coming break all pointed the same way.

The paper gives the worsening picture behind its own headline, fact by fact. For readers, it marks the month the agency's tone changed for good. Earlier reports had still weighed chances and options with some hope. This one records a slide that analysts no longer thought could be turned back. It dates that bleak judgment with care.
cia-0000135804: Orders from Lincoln fill a CIA cable dated May 3, 1954. Lincoln was the code name for the base running the Guatemala operation. The cable carries both working orders and general guidance for the field. Its own headline grammar stumbles, a flaw kept from the original. Orders from Lincoln were the marching orders of the campaign. The short cable keeps them as sent.
cia-0000135904: The CIA document from 1 April 1954 deals with acts of force planned for the days before D-day, in a file now declassified. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136104: The cable dated 5 March 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with MT/4, a two-part code standing alone as the whole subject of a Lincoln cable. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136204: With a date of 5 May 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a meeting between Calligeris and Estrada. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136304: LINCOLN asked for authority to strike in this June 1954 PBSUCCESS cable, reporting that a setback at Chiquimula that morning made action by the army in the capital more likely. The station proposed a strike the next day by three fighter aircraft, calling it an impressive show against a military, isolated, and easy-to-identify target ringed by a moat. Timing mattered, the cable argues, so the cause and effect would be read the right way.
cia-0000136404: Names of people who know about communist infiltration fill this January 1954 cable. It went to the senior representative at LINCOLN. The names were offered as possible help. One man is an agent living abroad. He made recent trips to Guatemala. Another is a former White Russian. He keeps contact with refugee groups arriving in Cuba. He picked up word on penetrations there. Contact runs through still other named persons. The names themselves stay withheld as IDENs.
cia-0000136904: Fuzz up the question of official backing, headquarters instructs LINCOLN in this May 1954 cable on deception and confusion activities. Reports keep arriving of a figure boasting of official United States backing, and those boasts are cutting into knowledge the operation wants blurred. With future Guatemalan charges in mind, it is particularly desirable to confuse them as to the sources of financial and other backing. The cable orders deliberate muddiness about who was paying for the rebellion.
cia-0000140404: Experiment in the field, not the laboratory. This April 1955 paper on hypnotism and covert operations argues that course. Academic experts are often too pessimistic, the writer says. Their caution rests on very few cases. Agency experimenters contradict much of it. He has personally witnessed responses that respected experts called impossible. Book knowledge feels cramped and closed-in to him. Evidence does not yet prove hypnotism a workable covert weapon. Only field tests can show what works, he argues.
un-ga-res-2504:
West New Guinea's fate was sealed in Resolution 2504, adopted by the General Assembly on 19 November 1969. The Dutch and Indonesia had settled their fight over the land in a 1962 deal. The UN ran the land for a short spell, then passed control to Indonesia. Under the deal, the people were to have an act of free choice on their future, with UN advice and help.

The Assembly now had the report on how that act was run in 1969, and on its result: a vote for life within Indonesia. The text takes note of the report and of the Secretary-General's role in the whole affair. Critics at the time, and since, have called the act far from free.
un-sc-res-1104: With a catalog date of 1997, Resolution 1104 records a decision of the UN Security Council. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1304: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 1304, which the catalog dates to 2000. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1504: Resolution 1504, a Security Council act of 2003, is preserved here in official-record form through English Wikisource. Such decisions can renew missions, tighten sanctions, or call parties to account, and all of them share one format. The entry keeps that format intact, findings first and operative clauses after, exactly as the members voted it.
un-sc-res-1604: Kept as Resolution 1604, a Security Council decision survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. The body that issues these texts sits at UN headquarters and votes as fifteen national delegations. Their agreed words, preserved here without trimming, are what later arguments about the Council's intent always return to in the end.
un-sc-res-1704:
Timor-Leste, the small Southeast Asian country that won independence in 2002, fell into unrest in 2006 when its security forces split. Resolution 1704 answered by establishing a new United Nations mission there. The mission's core strength was police rather than soldiers.

Inside the text, UN police are tasked with restoring public safety while local officers are rebuilt and retrained. The mission also supports elections, courts, and government offices across the young state. The resolution shows the Council doing quiet nation-building work, years after the crisis that first brought peacekeepers to Timor.
cia-0000135604: A Spanish-language document dated 2 September 1960 survives among the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force the CIA was training for an invasion of Cuba. September 1960 fell in the brigade's early buildup, well before the April 1961 landing. The catalog record gives no subject or author for this item. Readers who know Spanish can judge its contents directly; the title alone supports no more than its date, its language, and the file it belongs to.
cia-0000136704: A Spanish document dated 4 August 1960, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force. August 1960 fell in the brigade's first training season; the unit had been formed only that year. The catalog record names no subject for this item. It survives in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, an early dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from the operation's first summer.
plos-pone-0000004:
Douglas Strathdee, Helen Ibbotson, and Seth Grant asked a practical question about mouse genetics in work published by PLOS ONE in 2006. Gene engineers often park an added gene at the Gt(ROSA)26Sor locus, a safe harbor site in the mouse genome. The team tested whether the inserted gene works the same in either direction.

Their finding sits in the title: expression depends on orientation. A transgene facing one way at that locus behaved differently from the same gene facing the other way. For labs building mouse models of human disease, that is a warning worth knowing before the animals are bred. Design the insert carelessly, and the experiment can mislead from the start.
un-sc-res-704:
Security Council Resolution 704, adopted on August 9, 1991, recommended the Marshall Islands for membership in the United Nations. The Pacific island nation had lately closed a long period under United States administration, first as a trust territory after the war. Full self-rule under its compact with Washington freed it to seek its own seat in the world body.

The Assembly admitted the Marshall Islands on September 17, in a batch of new members freed by the Cold War's end. For a land of low atolls with a small population, the seat mattered. It gave the islands a direct voice on oceans, fishing, and the nuclear tests once carried out on their soil.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d104: Ambassador Winant wrote to Roosevelt from London on November 8, 1943, and the letter is Document 104 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant's reports in the final pre-summit weeks carried the mood of Churchill's government as the British party readied its own journey. The record supplies the date and the two men and nothing narrower. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' November run.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d204:
President Roosevelt sent Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek a personal, secret message on 10 November 1943 about the new long-range bombers America hoped to base in China. With them, he writes, heavy attacks on vital targets in Japan itself could begin much sooner than once seemed possible.

The plan needs five airfields for the big new planes in the Chengtu area, with basic housing, ready by the end of March 1944. America would supply the engineering skill, but Chiang must provide the labor and materials so the air supply line is not drained. Roosevelt offers Lend-Lease funds to speed the work, and promises a sudden, crippling blow against Japan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d304:
James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, answered President Roosevelt's urgent landing craft telegram on 24 November 1943. Working from Bureau of Shipping predictions, his message is mostly tables, listing how far one building program, program C, could be raised in each month from January to May.

The pattern is the same across the craft types named, from the larger infantry landing craft down to small mechanized boats. No increase at all is possible in January. Then come small gains in February and March, growing through April and May. One type, the LCT-7, shows no increase in any of the five months. The figures gave Roosevelt the hard limits within which the Cairo and Tehran planners had to fit Overlord and every rival landing plan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d404:

Presented in Edwin Arnold's English translation, the Bhagavad Gita is a Hindu scripture that forms part of the great epic Mahabharata. Tradition attributes the larger work to Vyasa. Its scene is a battlefield, just before fighting begins, where the warrior Arjuna must face relatives and teachers among the opposing army.

Arjuna hesitates, and his charioteer Krishna answers him. Krishna, revealed as divine, teaches duty, selfless action, and devotion, urging Arjuna to act without being ruled by the results. Readers meet questions about work, death, the self, and God in a tense conversation rather than a sermon, which helps explain its lasting place in Hindu life.
tob-10804:
Lady Wilde, Oscar Wilde's mother, who wrote as Speranza, gathered Ireland's folk beliefs in Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms, and Superstitions of Ireland. She collected fairy legends, healing charms, omens, and keening songs from the peasantry she knew. The oral world she recorded was already vanishing in her lifetime.

Tales of the sidhe, banshees, sacred wells, and second sight sit beside practical charms for illness, love, and protection. Lady Wilde writes in vivid, sympathetic prose, treating storytellers as authorities rather than curiosities. Folklore collections like hers preserve, in print, what a culture once carried entirely in memory and voice.
tob-4004:
Desiderius Erasmus published The Praise of Folly in 1509, and John Wilson's translation presents his mock-encomium in classic English. Folly herself takes the podium, robed and belled, to praise her own influence over human affairs. Monks, theologians, schoolmen, kings, courtiers, and lovers all owe their happiness, she explains, to her.

The joke sharpens as Folly grows earnest about war, corruption, and empty ritual, stinging the powerful while delighting the humanists who first passed the book hand to hand. Luther's generation weaponized its laughter; Erasmus himself stayed ironic. As satire that helped prepare a reformation while disowning one, The Praise of Folly remains sly, learned, and very funny.
tob-9047-62704:
Precious stones close Pliny's Natural History in volume six of Bostock's translation. Diamonds, emeralds, pearls, and lesser gems each get a history: where they are found, how they are cut, and what powers people claim for them. Pliny enjoys exposing fakes and frauds in the gem trade.

With the stones, the thirty-seven books come to an end. The survey began with the heavens and ends with the smallest bright things dug from the earth. No other Roman work attempts so much. Bostock's six volumes give English readers the whole of antiquity's great storehouse of fact, fable, and shrewd comment.
tob-0104:
Fifteenth-century Bavaria produced the Munich Manual of Demonic Magic, a working magician's handbook in Latin. Its unknown compiler cared little for theory. Conjurations, experiments, and lists of spirits fill the pages, aimed at plain results: treasure found, love won, enemies checked.

The raw, practical tone sets it apart from loftier grimoires that preach about angels. Scholars value it as a true picture of late medieval magic in daily use. The only English version is Richard Kieckhefer's modern translation, which remains under copyright, so no public-domain text is attached to this entry. The manual's fame rests on its blunt honesty.
tob-9104:
Hume's thirteen Principal Upanishads stand here in a second record of the Harvard Sanskritist's one-volume classic. The Katha's dialogue with Death and the Chandogya's thou art that anchor the set. Students across a century have learned Hindu philosophy from Hume's translations and notes.

The texts range from brief verses to long prose dialogues between kings, wives, sons, and sages. All circle one claim: the self within and the ground of the world are the same. Verified from the 1919 edition scan, this copy keeps the standard student text in circulation. Few single volumes carry so much of a tradition's thought.
tob-13504:
Henry Cornelius Agrippa, a German scholar and physician, issued his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in the 1530s. The work sums up the learned magic of the Renaissance in one system. The copy here follows the complete 1898 English edition.

Book one treats natural magic, the hidden powers of things; book two, the heavens and their numbers; book three, divine names and ceremony. Agrippa draws on Kabbalah, astrology, and ancient philosophy to argue that all levels of the world answer each other. The spurious fourth book often travels with it. Few occult books have been mined as long or as widely.
podcast-dannyjones-Dwh6Oa-N_04:
Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 vanished in 2014, and a viral video years later claimed to show the plane surrounded by orbs and disappearing. Danny Jones hosts a contest over that footage: the visual effects artists of Corridor Crew against Ashton Forbes, the video's leading defender, arguing over what the clips actually show.

The format makes this episode unusual for the series: claim and forensic answer in the same room. The artists explain how the effects could be built, frame by frame, and Forbes answers their points. Listeners can watch a conspiracy claim tested by the people best qualified to fake it. Whatever verdict a listener reaches, the recording is a model of how such disputes should sound, and a rare case of the debunkers getting equal time on a believer-friendly show.
podcast-joerogan-hw-ibiz-M04:
Filmmaker Oliver Stone joins Joe Rogan for episode 1992 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Stone is the director of Platoon, JFK, and a string of films that fight the known tale of US power. His talks run long on war and lies.

Stone and Rogan talk film craft, the Kennedy case, and the tales the state tells of itself. Stone shares how his war years in Vietnam shaped each frame he shoots. Rogan gives him the long form to teach and rant. Listeners get a famed director in full voice. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated views.
thompson-devils-evil-spirits-babylonia-v:
The second volume of R. Campbell Thompson's Devils and Evil Spirits of Babylonia came out at London in 1904. Where volume one fought demons in general, this one turns to set sicknesses. Thompson again pairs English renderings with the cuneiform texts and full notes.

The chief series here are Asakki Marsuti, on fever sickness, Ti'i, and Luh-ka, plus mixed spells that fit no one series. Each spell treats illness as a spirit to be named and driven out. The volume rounds out the classic English source on Mesopotamian healing magic.
hus-letters-workman-pope-1904:
Jan Hus, the Bohemian reformer, was burned at Constance in 1415 after a trial for heresy. The Letters of John Hus, in the 1904 English rendering by Herbert Workman and Martin Pope, gathers his full correspondence. His letters from prison at Constance form the heart of the book.

Hus writes to friends, backers, and the faithful at Prague, holding firm as the court closes in. The captivity letters show a man who knows the fire waits and will not bend. They are the key record of his trial told from inside the cell. Few martyrs of the age speak so plainly for themselves.
gospel-of-thomas-oxyrhynchus-fragments-1:
Egyptian sand kept three scraps of a lost gospel for some fifteen centuries. The Oxyrhynchus Sayings of Jesus, edited by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt in 1904, prints those Greek fragments with English renderings. In 1945 the full Gospel of Thomas came to light, and these scraps proved to be parts of it.

The sayings are short, sharp words of Jesus, with no birth tale, cross, or empty tomb around them. Scholars of 1904 knew only these pieces and argued hard over their age and worth. The pamphlet is the sole public-domain edition of the Thomas pieces. It shows a famous gospel at the hour of its first return.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-04:
The fourth number of The Equinox came out in September 1910, fat with the work of half a year. Crowley's journal had become a fixture of the London occult world by then. Each number aimed to be a small library of the order's mind.

Rites and holy books appear in these pages in their first print form. Around them stand poems, tales, and sharp reviews of rival works. The mix was the point: magic as a whole life of the mind. This number keeps the founding record of Thelema thick and rich throughout. It rewards any reader who opens it at random.
bullen-denizens-of-the-deep-1904:
Bullen returned to the deep in 1904 with a book on the life of the open ocean. Denizens of the Deep treats sea serpents and ocean monsters from a sailor's long watch. Frank Bullen had spent his youth before the mast on whalers and traders.

He weighs the serpent tales by what he knows of squid, whales, and the tricks of light at sea. Some tales fall; some, he holds, stand past plain explaining. The book is the ocean's mystery as a working seaman saw it. It pairs with his whaling classic as a life's log of the deep.
james-ghost-stories-antiquary-1904:
Cambridge don M. R. James reshaped the ghost tale in Ghost Stories of an Antiquary, his first set, from 1904. His ghosts rise from old books, coins, prints, and church lore. A look or a touch wakes them. Then calm turns to dread.

Tales such as the curse on a count's line set his mold. Learn the lore, touch the old thing, pay the price. James wrote in a dry, sly voice that makes fear bite more. Later ghost tales still walk the path he cut. James read his tales aloud to friends at Yule by fire light. That warm start makes the cold dread in them feel all the more sharp.
petrie-methods-aims-archaeology-1904:
W. M. Flinders Petrie laid down the laws of the dig in Methods and Aims in Archaeology, his guide of 1904. Ere Petrie, most digs were hunts for gold and show pieces. He demands that each scrap be kept, drawn, and placed by its layer. A plain pot in place, he says, tells more than a loose gem.

Rules for camps, crews, notes, and print fill the guide. Young dig men learned their trade from it for years. It is the first true field guide of the craft. The laws in it still rule good work on site.
budge-gods-of-egyptians-vol-1-1904:
E. A. Wallis Budge set out the gods of Egypt in Vol. 1 of The Gods of the Egyptians, out in 1904. Budge kept the Egypt hoard at the great state vault in London. He drew on hymns, tomb texts, and carved walls in the tongue of the land. This tome takes up the chief gods, their forms, kin, and cult towns.

Beast heads, sun discs, and myths of birth and death fill each part. Budge writes for the keen lay fan, not just sages. The pair of tomes was the main English guide for years. This one starts it.
budge-gods-of-egyptians-vol-2-1904:
E. A. Wallis Budge rounds out his pantheon in Vol. 2 of The Gods of the Egyptians, out in 1904. The first tome gave the chief gods and their myths. Here come the rest: gods of towns, of the dead, of birth and flood, and the strange mixed forms that crowd the walls of tombs and shrines in the land.

Tales of Osiris and his kin get full room here. Lists and draws help fans keep the throng straight. The set as a whole is Budge's gift to lay fans. It put the whole throng in English hands.
davies-celtic-researches-1804:
Edward Davies, a Welsh cleric, wrote this study of the old Britons in 1804, five years before his book on druid rites. It was the first full try in the Romantic age to build a Celtic past in one scheme. He worked from Welsh verse, old tales, and stone works.

Davies traced the first Britons to the east and tied their faith to the druids. He read names, myths, and rites as clues to one lost world of belief. Later scholars set much of it aside, but the book set the form for Celtic studies.
wood-n-rays-1904:
Robert W. Wood, an American physicist, paid a short call to Blondlot's lab at Nancy in 1904. The French lab claimed to show N rays, a new ray that most men outside France now doubted. Wood wrote this short letter to Nature on what he saw and did there.

In the dark, Wood took a key part from the ray tool and put it in his pocket. The lab men still read the ray's marks just as before, with the tool broke and blind. His letter, three hours of work in sum, burst the N ray craze at one blow.
duckworth-morphology-anthropology-1904:
W. L. H. Duckworth, a Cambridge scholar of the body, wrote this text book on form and the study of man in 1904. It joins two themes: the shapes of ape and man, and the rise of man from ape kin. Cambridge men used it to teach the new field.

Duckworth sets out skulls, brains, and bones of apes and men side by side. He then turns to the fossil finds known in his day and fits them in the line of growth. The book forms a bridge from the living body to the claims for fossil man.
hinton-fourth-dimension-1904:
Charles Howard Hinton set out his full case for a fourth dimension in 1904. The book builds on his past work on cubes and higher space. Its 1912 print kept the work in wide use. Hinton was a math man with a deep bent for big thought.

He shows how a cube gains a new form, the tesseract, in four reaches of space. Tales, drills, and clear cuts help the mind grasp the leap. Hinton also asks what higher space means for faith and the self. The book stays his full plea for a world past our three reaches.
steiner-theosophy-1904:
Rudolf Steiner wrote his Theosophy in 1904, while he still led the German theosophists. Its full title calls it a first step to knowledge past the senses. The book sets out man as body, soul, and spirit. It is the root text of the school he later built, Anthroposophy.

Birth anew and karma frame the tale of the soul's long growth. Three worlds stack up: flesh, soul, and spirit, each with its own laws. Steiner then maps a path by which a pupil can gain sight of those worlds. The book asks for slow, keen thought, not blind faith.
troward-edinburgh-lectures-1904:
Thomas Troward gave his Edinburgh Lectures on Mental Science in 1904. Troward was a judge in India who turned to deep thought on mind. The talks give the strict case for New Thought. They are the most weighty of the mind science books.

Spirit and mind drive the growth of form in his scheme. The mind of man shares in the mind that made all things, he holds. Thought, thus, is a real force that shapes fate and flesh. The talks set the creed of a whole school on firm, clear ground.
wells-food-of-the-gods-1904:
H. G. Wells wrote The Food of the Gods in 1904. Two men of science brew a food that makes all life grow vast. They call it Herakleophorbia and test it on chicks and wasps at a farm. The food leaks to the wild, and rats and weeds grow to dread size.

A race of giant babes grows up in a world not made for them. Wells tells their tale with warmth as well as dread of scale. Crowds cheer the giants, then fear them and seek their end. The tale asks what growth means when it will not stop.
defoe-the-storm-1704:
Daniel Defoe published The Storm in 1704, an eyewitness collection on the Great Storm of 1703. The book is often called the first work of modern journalism in English prose writing. Defoe advertised for accounts and wove his own survey into a national record of loss.

The storm of November 1703 sank ships, unroofed churches, and killed thousands across southern England in one night. Defoe prints letters from ports and parishes, lists of wrecked men-of-war, and chimneys down in London. He weighs natural causes against providence, and scolds both scoffers and panicked preachers of the day in print. Eddystone Lighthouse fell with its builder inside, a loss the book records in stark detail for readers. Its method, gather testimony fast and print it plain, set a pattern for news.
london-sea-wolf-1904:
Jack London published The Sea-Wolf in 1904, his novel of a shipwrecked intellectual brutalized into manhood at sea. A seal-hunting schooner ruled by the terrifying Captain Wolf Larsen carries the tale. London, who had sailed those waters, loaded the book with sea craft and his creed.

Humphrey van Weyden, a critic and gentleman, is picked up from a ferry wreck and made a cabin boy by Larsen. Larsen, a superman of body and nihilist brain, crushes mutiny, reads Milton, and argues that life is yeast and appetite. Maud Brewster, a poet cast away in turn, joins Humphrey in escape to an island and a slow, tender stand against despair. Larsen, blinded by headaches, dies unbowed, and the pair are rescued from Endeavor Island at the close. The debates between captain and critic still give the sea tale its voltage.
conrad-nostromo-1904:
Joseph Conrad published Nostromo in 1904, a large novel set in Costaguana, a made-up country in South America. A silver mine drives the plot and draws in foreign money and local politics. Nostromo is an Italian sailor trusted by all sides. Revolutions rise and fall around the mine and the port town of Sulaco.

Conrad follows many figures, from mine owners to rebels and their families. Silver brings wealth, but it also brings betrayal and death. Nostromo himself is changed by the trust placed in him. Readers prize the book as a vast and clear-eyed account of empire, greed, and power.
pirandello-late-mattia-pascal-1904:
Luigi Pirandello published The Late Mattia Pascal in 1904, an Italian novel about a man freed by a mistake. Mattia Pascal leaves his unhappy home and his debts behind. While away, he reads that a drowned man has been named as him. Everyone at home thinks he is dead.

Mattia takes a new name and tries to start a fresh life. He soon finds that a man with no past has no rights and no real place. Love and money both slip from his grasp. He returns home to find his wife remarried. The novel mixes comedy and sadness in its study of identity.
reymont-peasants-1904:
Wladyslaw Reymont wrote The Peasants as a four-volume Polish epic, published in the first years of the 1900s. The Knopf English text of 1928 gathers the work in one volume. Life in the village of Lipce follows the four seasons. Land, faith, weddings, and feuds shape the peasants' year.

The Boryna family stands at the center, with land disputes and a tangled marriage plot. Reymont writes of soil and weather as forces in their own right. Village speech and custom fill the pages with color. The epic helped Reymont win the Nobel Prize in 1924. It remains Poland's great novel of rural life.
adams-mont-saint-michel-1904:
In 1904 Henry Adams published a study of two great churches of medieval France, Mont Saint Michel and Chartres. He wrote it first for his nieces, in a warm and personal voice. Adams had already toured both sites and knew their stones and stories well. The book treats stone, glass, and prayer as one work of art.

Adams reads the abbey and the cathedral as signs of a world held together by faith in the Virgin Mary. He sets that unity against the split and driven world he knew in his own time. Lovers of Gothic building still turn to it as a classic guide.
veblen-business-enterprise-1904:
Thorstein Veblen was a Norwegian-American economist famous for mocking the rich in his Theory of the Leisure Class. His 1904 Theory of Business Enterprise turns from manners to machines and markets. It asks who really runs modern industry, and for what ends.

Veblen sets the captain of industry, who chases profit and credit, against the engineer, who wants goods made well. Business, he argues, often profits by holding back output rather than by serving need. His clash of profit and workmanship became a founding charge of institutional economics. The book's dry wit makes its hard economics easier to take. It followed his Leisure Class by five years and deepened its attack.
bahai-kitab-iqan-1904:
Baha'u'llah, founder of the Baha'i faith, wrote the Kitab-i-Iqan, The Book of Certitude, in Baghdad in the early 1860s. Ali Kuli Khan made this first English translation, published in 1904. The work stands as the faith's foundational treatise on its central doctrine.

That doctrine is progressive revelation: God sends teachers age by age, each renewing religion for a changed world. The book reads Jewish, Christian, and Muslim scriptures as one unfolding story pointing toward its author's own claim. Baha'i readers still study it as the surest guide to their founder's thought. It was written in answer to questions raised by a learned uncle of the Bab.
crowley-mathers-goetia-of-solomon-1904:
The Goetia, in the 1904 edition translated by Mathers and introduced by Crowley, is the first printed edition of the first book of the Lemegeton. The Lemegeton, or Lesser Key of Solomon, is a grimoire, a handbook of ceremonial magic ascribed to King Solomon. Mathers worked from manuscripts in the British Museum.

The text lists seventy-two spirits, with their seals, ranks, offices, and the hours and tools for calling them. Crowley's introduction frames the spirits as forces of the human brain rather than as literal demons. The edition defined modern ceremonial magic's demonology and set the pattern for later occult publishing.
basil-valentine-triumphal-chariot-of-ant:
The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, in Waite's 1893 translation, presents the classic antimony treatise ascribed to Basil Valentine. Valentine, a supposed fifteenth-century monk, lent his name to a shelf of Paracelsian writings. Antimony, a brittle metal-like substance, was the wonder drug of that school.

The treatise praises antimony's powers to purge and cure, and gives the furnace work for preparing its many forms. Its title pictures the metal riding in triumph over the diseases that resist common medicines. Paracelsian doctors treated the book as their pharmacopoeia, their official guide to a prized and dangerous remedy.
newton-opticks-1704:
Isaac Newton published Opticks in 1704, a treatise on the reflections, refractions, inflections, and colours of light. Unlike the Principia, Newton wrote Opticks in English and built it from experiments readers could picture. Prisms, slits, and dark rooms are its stage.

Newton showed that white light splits into colors and joins again, proving color lies in light itself, not in the glass. He measured the bending of rays and studied the rings now named for him. Closing queries speculated on gravity, matter, and God's role in nature. The book founded physical optics and set a model for experimental science: ask nature plain questions and record exact answers.
smith-wealth-nations-cannan-1904:
Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations appears here in Edwin Cannan's 1904 edition. Smith, a Scottish philosopher, first published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in 1776. Cannan, an economist, edited the text with notes that scholars used for a century.

Smith argued that the division of labor makes nations rich, and that free trade beats the old mercantilist controls. His famous invisible hand pictured each person seeking gain yet serving the public good. He also warned about monopolies, dull factory work, and business plots against the public. The book founded modern economics, and Cannan's edition remains a careful way to read it in full.
hammurabi-code-harper-1904:
Robert Francis Harper published his translation of The Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon in 1904. Hammurabi ruled Babylon in the 1700s BCE, and his laws were carved on a stone pillar found in Persia in 1901. Harper, a scholar at the University of Chicago, gave English readers the full text.

Some 282 laws cover trade, wages, marriage, injury, and slavery, often with the famous measure of an eye for an eye. Penalties differ by the rank of the persons involved, a window into Babylonian society. The code is the oldest complete legal code known. Harper's translation made it a standard source for law schools and historians alike.
suess-face-of-earth-vol1-sollas-1904:
W J Sollas published his translation of Volume 1 of Eduard Suess's Face of the Earth in 1904. Suess, a Viennese geologist, wrote Das Antlitz der Erde as a synthesis of the whole science. Sollas, an Oxford geologist, carried the great work into English over many years.

Volume 1 treats the structure of the continents and the history of the Mediterranean lands. Suess argued that mountains rise as the cooling Earth contracts and its crust crumples, the contraction theory of mountain building. He also named Gondwana, a lost southern continent pieced together from matching fossils and rocks. The volume began the English form of the most ambitious geology of its age.
marlowe-doctor-faustus-1604:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus near the end of his short life. He drew on German tales of a scholar who bargained with the devil. The play reached print in 1604, eleven years after Marlowe's death. It became the defining English tragedy of the overreaching mind.

Faustus, bored with law, medicine, and theology, sells his soul for twenty-four years of magic and pleasure. A good angel and a bad angel fight for him while devils stage shows and tricks. The years slip away in pranks until the final hour arrives. Faustus's last speech, begging time to stop, remains one of the most powerful scenes in English drama.
swift-battle-of-the-books-1704:
Jonathan Swift wrote The Battle of the Books while working as secretary to Sir William Temple, a retired statesman. A loud quarrel then divided scholars: were modern writers the equals of the ancient Greeks and Romans? Swift published his mock-epic prose satire in 1704, alongside A Tale of a Tub.

In the royal library at St. James, the ancient and modern books come alive and go to war. Bees and spiders argue the same case in a famous fable: the spider spins from itself, the bee gathers from every flower. Swift mocks pedants on both sides but saves his sharpest cuts for modern pride. The piece remains the wittiest shot fired in the ancients-versus-moderns war.
swift-tale-of-a-tub-1704:
Jonathan Swift published A Tale of a Tub in 1704, his first major work, issued with The Battle of the Books. Swift was then an unknown Irish clergyman in his thirties. The book's wild energy and strange digressions startled readers and made his reputation.

The tale itself is an allegory of three brothers who inherit coats they must not alter, standing for the Catholic, Anglican, and dissenting churches. Around it Swift piles mock prefaces and digressions praising madness and modern learning. The satire cuts at religious corruption and empty scholarship alike. Many call it the most savage and brilliant prose satire of its age.
synge-riders-to-sea-1904:
J. M. Synge drew Riders to the Sea from his visits to the Aran Islands, where the sea took men from nearly every family. The one-act play was first performed in 1904. It lasts under an hour and is often called the summit of Irish tragedy.

Maurya, an old widow, has already lost her husband and four sons to the sea. The play opens as her daughters identify a drowned man's clothing from far up the coast. Her last surviving son, Bartley, insists on sailing despite her pleas. When his body is carried in, Maurya reaches a calm, terrible acceptance. Synge's language, shaped by Irish speech, gives the grief a biblical weight.
james-golden-bowl-1904:
Henry James published The Golden Bowl in 1904, the last great novel he completed. James wrote it in his densest late style, where a raised eyebrow can carry a chapter's weight. He took the title image from Ecclesiastes: a golden bowl, beautiful and ready to crack.

American millionaire Adam Verver buys his daughter Maggie a husband, the Italian Prince Amerigo, and then marries the prince's former lover, Charlotte. Father and daughter are so close that the two outsiders drift back together. Maggie slowly perceives the affair and, without a single scene of accusation, maneuvers to win her husband back. The novel is James's most architectonic work, built like the bowl itself: flawless, and full of strain.
schiller-wilhelm-tell-1804:
William Tell was Schiller's last completed play, finished in 1804, and Theodore Martin translated it into English. Tell, a Swiss marksman and quiet family man, refuses to bow to the hat of the Austrian bailiff Gessler. Gessler's punishment is cruel: Tell must shoot an apple from his own son's head.

Tell succeeds, yet vows revenge, and the Swiss cantons rise against their rulers. Schiller turns the old legend into a broad drama of a people's freedom. The play made Tell a worldwide emblem of resistance to tyranny. Rossini's opera later carried the tale further still. Schiller wrote it without ever seeing Switzerland, working from chronicles and maps alone.
hesse-peter-camenzind-1904:
Peter Camenzind, Hermann Hesse's first successful novel, appeared in German in 1904. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Peter grows up in a Swiss mountain village, loses his mother young, and leaves to seek the life of a writer.

Cities, love affairs, and friendships fail to give Peter the belonging he craves. He drinks, drifts, and returns at last toward home and a simpler duty. Hesse fills the tale with Alpine weather, lakes, and long walks. The novel made his name in Germany at age twenty-seven. Its themes of seeking and homecoming run through all his later work.
andreyev-red-laugh-1904:
The Red Laugh reached English in Alexandra Linden's translation, first issued in 1905 from Leonid Andreyev's Russian of 1904. The book calls itself fragments of a discovered manuscript. An officer in the Russo-Japanese War records heat, thirst, shellfire, and madness in broken notes that slide toward vision.

The red laugh itself is his name for the grinning horror of the war as a whole. A second part follows his brother home, where peace proves as haunted as the front. Andreyev wrote before war literature had a modern form, and he found one in fever and fragment. The book became an early landmark of anti-war writing in Europe. Its method shaped later expressionist prose.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-04:
Volume four of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night came out in 1885 with the rest of the main set. Shahrazad's sister Dinarzad keeps asking for one more tale before dawn. The king keeps listening, and the pile of stories within stories grows deeper with every night.

Burton renders the Arabic with deliberate closeness, keeping proverbs, verses, and oaths intact. His notes on law, custom, and daily life in the East fill the margins of the text. The middle volumes of the set reward steady readers most: patterns of fate and cleverness repeat with fresh faces. Burton printed the work for subscribers, since its frankness barred the open market.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
Burton's fourth supplemental volume, issued in the late 1880s, continues his gathering of Nights tales from side manuscripts. By this point the project had become the largest English rendering of Arabic story ever attempted. The tales here extend Shahrazad's world with fresh kings, quests, and enchantments in her familiar manner.

Burton's notes remain a second book running under the first, full of parallels from his travels. He served in India, Arabia, and Africa, and his comparisons draw on all three. The Gutenberg text of this volume is ebook 3448. Few Victorian translations match this one's stamina. Volume four keeps the supplement's standard: nothing cut, nothing softened, everything annotated.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume four of The Ocean of Story, from Penzer's ten-volume edition begun in 1924, continues Tawney's rendering of Somadeva. The Kathasaritsagara now braids its hero's fortunes with tale cycles told by sages, wives, and wandering ascetics. Every narrator opens a new door, and behind it waits another narrator with a stranger tale.

Somadeva wrote to divert a queen, and diversion remains the law of the book. Penzer's notes in this volume chase the tale of the grateful beasts and other wanderers across three continents. The translation's calm surface over such abundance is Tawney's quiet triumph. Readers may dip anywhere and surface with a complete story. The ocean, by design, has no dull stretches for long.
kent-lectures-homoeopathic-materia-medic:
James Tyler Kent published his Lectures on Homoeopathic Materia Medica in 1904, from lectures given at the Post-Graduate School of Homoeopathics. The first edition staged here is the Calcutta printing of Roy Publishing House. Kent, an American physician, became the defining voice of classical homeopathy in the United States.

Remedy by remedy, from Abies to Zincum, he pictures the patient type each medicine fits: symptoms, temperament, and all. His vivid drug pictures taught generations of homeopaths how to prescribe. The remedy lectures are complete in this scan, though its printed index breaks off at Carbo veg. in the final leaves. Kent's book remains a working manual for practitioners of his school. Few medical lectures have been so often reprinted.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-04:
The fourth volume of Charles Thomson's Bible, from 1808, holds the New Testament. Thomson translated it from the Greek, as he had the Septuagint in the first three volumes. Jane Aitken printed the set at Philadelphia, and it counts as the first American translation of the whole Bible into English.

The four gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and the other apostles, and Revelation stand in Thomson's plain, careful English. His renderings sometimes cut closer to the Greek than the King James text does. Thomson had been secretary of Congress through the war for independence. His Bible is both a work of faith and a monument of early American print culture.
bernard-clairvaux-letters-1904:
Bernard of Clairvaux ruled half of Europe from his abbey by letter, and Samuel J. Eales chose and translated a set of those letters in 1904. Bernard wrote to popes, kings, bishops, monks, and his own kin, in a voice that could scold, soothe, and blaze on one page. The letters span his wars for church reform and the launching of the Second Crusade.

Readers meet the abbot rebuking luxury, defending his friend Abelard's enemies and attacking Abelard himself, and mourning the crusade's failure. His style is a river of scripture turned to daily business. The selection shows the man behind the saint: tender to novices, iron to princes. Eales adds notes to place each letter in its fight.
scheible-das-kloster-vol04:
In 1846 Johann Scheible issued band four of Das Kloster, holding cells thirteen through sixteen. The German anthology had grown past its first year into a known fixture of the trade. Scheible, its editor and publisher, hunted down scarce print that libraries had long ignored.

What he found, he reprinted whole: grimoires, Faust books, and grim Höllenzwänge among them. Folk charms, some meant for love and some for healing, share the binding with popular tales. The worth of such a band lies in survival. Texts that lived in a handful of copies now sat in one sturdy volume on many shelves.
fries-system-philosophie-1804:
Jakob Friedrich Fries issued his System der Philosophie als evidente Wissenschaft in German in 1804. The title presents philosophy as a science built on clear, self evident ground. Fries worked in Kant's shadow and reshaped Kant's teaching for his own school. His followers became known as the Friesian school.

Fries sought the roots of knowledge in the structure of the mind itself. He held that careful inner study could show why our basic beliefs must hold. The system covers knowing, acting, and faith in one frame. German readers kept his name alive through the century. The original text shows Kant's legacy taking a new path.
thomson-electricity-matter-1904:
Lectures given at Yale in 1903 as the Silliman Lectures became J. J. Thomson's Electricity and Matter in 1904. Thomson had discovered the electron, a particle far lighter than any atom, in 1897. His lectures present the corpuscular theory, which treats electrons as the basic bits of matter. Cathode rays figure large in the evidence.

Thomson shows how his particles can explain electric charge, mass, and the build of atoms. He writes as a guide at the front of a new field. The lectures carry the excitement of a science remaking itself. Readers see theory built straight from lab results. The book fixed his views for a wide public.
kelvin-baltimore-lectures-1904:
Lord Kelvin gave twenty lectures at Johns Hopkins in 1884, and they appeared in print in 1904. The Baltimore Lectures treat molecular dynamics and the wave theory of light. Kelvin built mechanical models to picture how the ether might carry light waves. Twelve appendices extend the lectures with later work and corrections.

Kelvin thinks aloud here, testing models, noting doubts, and pushing analogies hard. His pages show a great physicist before quantum and relativity changed the field. The ether models failed in the end, yet the effort taught much. Historians value the lectures as a record of classical physics at its height. The style stays vivid throughout.
nernst-theoretical-chemistry-palmer-1904:
Walther Nernst systematized physical chemistry in his Theoretical Chemistry, Englished by L. M. Palmer in 1904. The English text was the second edition, drawn from the fourth German edition. The subtitle names his twin guides: Avogadro's rule and thermodynamics. Together they frame his account of matter and its changes.

Nernst applies heat theory to solutions and to electrochemistry in depth. Readers learn how energy rules reactions, cells, and the balance between states. His path here leads toward his later heat theorem, the third law of thermodynamics. The book served as the field's great textbook for years. Its order and scope set a standard.
osler-aequanimitas-1904:
Osler's Aequanimitas gathers his addresses to medical students, nurses, and doctors, first printed in 1904. The title essay praises calm steadiness, the quality its Latin name describes. Osler believed a doctor's temper shapes a patient's trust. His talks mix practical advice with wide reading and warm humor.

Other addresses in the volume treat study, books, and the conduct of a medical life. Generations of students received the book at graduation as a kind of charge. Its essays became the most quoted medical humanism in English. Osler writes as a mentor who expects much and scolds gently. The volume keeps his voice alive. Readers outside medicine enjoy it too.
osler-science-immortality-1904:
William Osler delivered Science and Immortality as the Ingersoll Lecture in 1904. The lecture series asked speakers to address human immortality from their own field. Osler, a leading doctor and teacher, brought a clinical eye to the old question. He asks what science can and cannot say about survival after death.

He sorts people into groups by their stance toward the question. Some hold faith, some doubt, and some rest in calm acceptance. Osler treats each stance with respect and dry wit. His own position stays modest and humane. The address became his most famous piece of philosophy. It shows medicine thinking about its limits.
spr-proceedings-vol18-1903-1904:
Volume eighteen binds parts forty six through forty nine, for 1903 and 1904. Two decades in, the SPR Proceedings keep their founding bargain. Print the evidence for telepathy, apparitions, and mediumship, and print the criticism too. Fresh experiments try to close the gaps critics had found.

Trance cases, with Piper still central, receive long verbatim reports. The census tradition shapes new surveys of spontaneous experiences. Physical wonders appear rarely, and then under heavy guard. Volume eighteen sustains the journal of record through its Edwardian years. It offers historians a dense, dated file of the debate. The society's patience is its signature here.
scott-elliot-lost-lemuria-1904:
The Lost Lemuria, printed in 1904, gives Scott-Elliot's account of the sunken southern continent. Lemuria, in theosophical teaching, preceded Atlantis as a home of early humanity. Scott-Elliot marshals geological and biological evidence for the lost land. The spread of fossils and living species across oceans anchors his case.

Two maps trace the continent and its shrinking remains. He joins the science of his day to the society's clairvoyant records. The Story of Atlantis is the companion volume to this one. Together they set out the Theosophical Society's lost continent doctrine in full. The Gutenberg text preserves the argument entire. It remains the movement's Lemuria in chief.
flaubert-sentimental-education-dunne-190:
Frédéric Moreau drifts through Paris in Flaubert's Sentimental Education, loving a married woman from afar and finishing little he starts. The M. Walter Dunne translation of 1904 presents the novel complete in both volumes. Revolution breaks out in 1848 around Frédéric, yet even history cannot stir him to act.

Flaubert builds the great anti-Bildungsroman, a tale of education that teaches its hero nothing he can use. Friends rise, scheme, and fall while Frédéric watches, always a step behind his own life. Critics rank the book among the finest French novels, a cold, exact portrait of a wasted generation.
flaubert-bouvard-pecuchet-dunne-1904:
Two Paris copy clerks inherit money, quit their desks, and set out to master all knowledge in Bouvard and Pécuchet. Flaubert left the novel unfinished at his death, and the Dunne translation of 1904 gives it complete in both parts. Farming, chemistry, medicine, and love each defeat the pair in turn.

Their failures pile up into a black comedy of human folly, aimed at every sure system of the age. Flaubert, who read hundreds of books to write it, mocks the very learning he gathered. The pair end where they began, copying, which may be the bleakest joke in French fiction.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol04:
By 1857 the Journal of Discourses had reached Volume IV, still printed at Liverpool for Saints on two continents. Shorthand men recorded Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve Apostles, and others as they preached in Utah. The sermons range from first principles of the faith to sharp words on daily behavior.

Read as a whole, the volume shows a church settling doctrine while building towns in a hard land. The doctrinal record unfolds sermon by sermon, year by year, in the leaders' own phrasing. Scholars and Saints alike return to these pages when they want the era undiluted.
russell-new-creation-vol6-1904:
Russell closed his own series with The New Creation, the sixth Studies volume of 1904, written for the consecrated. The book treats the calling, holiness, and discipline of the new creature, the believer set apart for God's work. Church order, conduct, marriage, and daily duty all fall under its careful, detailed rules.

Where earlier volumes mapped history and prophecy, this one governs a daily life from waking to sleep. Russell writes as pastor and organizer, shaping a people fit for the kingdom he expected very soon. With it his six-volume set stands complete, the full system of the Bible Student movement in its founder's words.
pargiter-markandeya-purana-1904:
F. Eden Pargiter translated the Markandeya Purana for the Bibliotheca Indica series, completing the English text in 1904 after years of work. The Purana ranks among the oldest of its kind in India, and its crown is the Devi Mahatmya, the great hymn to the Goddess. Kings, sages, cosmic ages, and the deeds of gods fill the frame around that core.

In the Devi Mahatmya the Goddess rises to fight demons no god can master, and she wins in glory. That section shaped goddess worship across India and is still sung aloud at her festivals today. Pargiter's careful version remains the standard scholarly English rendering of the whole Purana for students.
nassau-fetichism-in-west-africa-1904:
Robert Hamill Nassau summed up forty years on the Gabon coast in Fetichism in West Africa, published in 1904. Nassau, an American Presbyterian missionary and physician, observed native customs across the Ogowe region for decades. Fetishism, in his term, witchcraft, and secret societies form the heart of his account.

He writes as a convinced missionary, yet also as a careful witness who learned languages and sat in village councils. Tales, trials, and charms fill pages drawn from life rather than books. The volume stands as a major period record of religion on the Gabon coast, to be read with its era in mind.
howitt-the-native-tribes-of-south-east-a:
Alfred William Howitt devoted his life to the peoples of the southeast, and The Native Tribes of South-East Australia of 1904 is his magnum opus. The Kurnai, Wiradjuri, and neighboring nations fill its pages. Kinship systems, initiation ceremonies, and magic stand at the center of his lifelong record.

Howitt learned from Aboriginal elders over decades, in an age when few settlers listened at all. His marriage classes and clan rules became building blocks of kinship theory worldwide. The book stands as the fullest early account of the southeast tribes, gathered by a patient friend of their old men.
stevenson-the-zuni-indians-1904:
Matilda Coxe Stevenson was among the first women to do serious fieldwork in the Southwest, and she spent years at Zuni Pueblo. Her report, published in 1904 in the Bureau of American Ethnology's annual report, is the fullest early study of Zuni religion.

Stevenson describes the rain priesthood, whose prayers served the whole pueblo, and the kachina cult with its masked dancers. She gives detailed accounts of the esoteric fraternities, the secret societies that ran ceremonies and healing. Her access to restricted rites raised questions even then. Whatever the disputes, the record she left is unmatched in detail.
rutherford-radio-activity-1904:
Ernest Rutherford published Radio-activity in 1904, only a few years after radioactivity itself was found. Rutherford, a New Zealand physicist working in Canada and England, was the field's boldest experimenter. His book was the first full textbook on the new science.

Rutherford explains rays from uranium and radium, and how one element can change into another. He sets out half-life, the steady rate at which active matter decays. The work helped turn a strange glow in the lab into nuclear science, the field Rutherford would lead for decades. It also gathers the lab methods used to trace rays and count particles.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol5-extra-190:
Hastings issued an extra fifth volume for his Dictionary of the Bible in 1904, two years after the main set closed. It gathers articles that arrived too late, plus fuller indexes and a map of Palestine. James Hastings meant the set to stay current.

The extra volume adds fresh work on topics like the Dead Sea region and new finds from excavation. Indexes of texts, names, and subjects bind all five volumes into one tool. Many sets in libraries lack this volume, which makes a complete run prized. It rounds out the greatest one-generation Bible dictionary in English.
plos-pone-0003404:
Danhua Jiang, Yuqi Wang, and Yizhong Wang studied flowering control in a small plant in 2008. The plant, Arabidopsis, times its blooms with a set of switch genes. One gene machine, called Polycomb repressive complex 2, turns genes off. The team tested its grip on two flowering genes.

Parts of the machine, named CLF and EMF2, helped hold both genes down. The genes are FLOWERING LOCUS C and FLOWERING LOCUS T. Keeping them off delays flowering until the right season. The work explains one brake plants use before they commit to bloom.
plos-pone-0003504:
Jacob Shun-Jen Yang, Jia-Min Bai, and Tzumin Lee traced protein delivery in fly neurons in this 2008 paper. Neurons sort membrane proteins to dendrites or axons, their two branch types. How that sorting is set up and kept was little known. The team followed one protein, Dscam, with a TM1 segment.

A motor complex called dynein-dynactin proved essential for its dendrite restriction. The motor hauls cargo along the cell's inner tracks. Without it, Dscam lost its proper branch address. The work exposes the shipping system behind neuron branch identity. Fruit flies remain a fast, cheap stand-in for basic neuron questions.
plos-pone-0003604:
Tao Yang, Juliet K. Knowles, and Qun Lu tested small protective molecules in this 2008 paper. Alzheimer's disease involves a toxic protein fragment called amyloid-beta, or Aβ. That fragment drives nerve cell death and synapse damage. A receptor called p75 NTR can mediate part of that harm.

The team used small, non-peptide ligands that bind p75 NTR. Those ligands inhibited Aβ-induced neurodegeneration in their tests. They also reduced the synaptic impairment the fragment causes. Drug-like blockers of this receptor point toward new Alzheimer's treatments. Amyloid is the best known target in Alzheimer's, yet drugs against it keep failing.
plos-pone-0003704:
Mari Kumashiro, Osamu Yokoyama, and Hidetoshi Ishibashi published this primate study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Eye contact and pointing are classic ways to direct another's attention to a target. The authors had earlier asked whether such joint attention relates to copying actions in Japanese monkeys.

Here they report that imitation of body movements was eased when joint attention came first. Eye contact and pointing set up a shared focus between monkey and human model. The result ties social attention to learning by copying in our primate cousins, a link also claimed for human children.
plos-pone-0003804:
Rogerio Meneghini, Abel L. Packer, and Lilian Nassi-Calò published this bibliometric study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Journal impact factor is widely taken as a mark of an article's relevance and quality. Peer review inside one journal is supposed to be uniform. The authors tested whether authors' country still shapes later citations.

They found articles by Latin American authors in prestigious journals receive fewer citations. The gap appears despite the same journals and review process. The finding exposes a geographic bias in how science notices and rewards its producers, with costs for researchers outside rich countries.
plos-pone-0003904:
Patricia Resa-Infante, Núria Jorba, Noelia Zamarreño, and co-authors studied how flu virus copies itself in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article focuses on the virus polymerase, its copying machine. That machine has three parts, PB1, PB2, and PA. It works inside the nucleus of infected cells.

PB2 helps decide which hosts a flu strain can infect. The team placed a tagged PB2 in human cells and pulled out its partners. They found that host importin proteins must engage PB2 for copying to proceed. Blocking that contact could offer a new angle for flu drugs. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004004:
Andreas C. Fröbius, David Q. Matus, and Elaine C. Seaver studied pattern genes in a marine worm in 2008. Hox genes assign body region identities along the head-to-tail axis. In many animals, their order on the chromosome matches their body order. That neat match is called colinearity.

Their PLOS ONE article examines Hox genes in the worm Capitella sp. I. They report both the genomic layout and where genes switch on. The worm belongs to a major animal branch with few such studies. Its pattern tests how universal Hox colinearity really is. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004104:
Keiko Takahashi, Sawako Yoshina, Maekawa Masashi, and co-authors studied a mental retardation gene in worms in 2009. PQBP1 is a causative gene for X-linked mental retardation. Patients with its mutations often show lean bodies. The worm C. elegans carries a strictly conserved version of the gene.

Their PLOS ONE article made glowing and mutant worms for that homologue. Analysis tied the gene to lipid metabolism in the animals. Fat handling may explain the lean build in patients. A simple worm thus models a human brain disorder's body signs. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004204:
Taeg Kim and Thomas Braciale published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells sit at body surfaces such as the skin, airways, and gut. There they start adaptive immune responses against germs and harmless substances alike. The respiratory tract holds several distinct subsets of these cells.

The authors compared how well each lung dendritic cell subset supports the induction of virus-specific killer CD8 T cells. They report that the subsets differ in this capacity. Knowing which subset does the heavy lifting helps vaccine designers aim at the right cell.
plos-pone-0004304:
Haguy Wolfenson and colleagues published this cell adhesion study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Focal adhesions are multi-protein complexes that link a cell to the matrix around it and let the cell sense that matrix. Much is known about their molecular composition, yet the rules governing their dynamics were less clear.

The authors examined the juxtamembrane cytoplasm, the cell interior just beneath these adhesions, and its role in adhesion behaviour. They show that this thin layer helps govern how focal adhesions move and remodel. A cell's grip on its surroundings, it turns out, is managed from just under the surface.
plos-pone-0004404: In 2009, a team found a busy protein with two jobs. Tollip mediated protein sumoylation beyond its known immune receptor role. The busy multi-tasker linked two tagging systems. The neat finding rewrites Tollip's job description. The extra role deepens cell-signaling maps today.
plos-pone-0004504: In 2009, Luo, Luo, and Xiong coaxed marrow cells toward insulin making. Cytokines drove bone marrow SCA+ cells into pancreatic islets, converting them toward insulin production. The marrow cells homed to islets. The finding hints at diabetes therapy. The conversion was partial.
plos-pone-0004604: In 2009, a team found cristae shaping molecular roams. Anomalous diffusion induced by cristae shape in the inner cell-power membrane was modeled. The folds slowed protein movement a whole lot. The finding maps cell-power function anew today. The shape is quite complex.
plos-pone-0004704: In 2009, Valverde, Célérier, and Baranyi linked an orphan receptor to mood anew. GPR3 receptor emerged as a novel actor in emotional-like responses. The brain receptor shaped mood quite strongly. The finding maps neurobiology research. The Gs signaling is constitutive.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-04:
With Volume 4, from 1897, the scene shifts from Acadia toward Quebec. Thwaites follows the mission as it moves to the great St. Lawrence River. Champlain's world and the first posts on the river come into clear view.

Jesuit eyes record the founding years of New France in fine detail. They describe trade, travel by canoe, and talks with Native nations. Hopes run high, yet money and men stay scarce each year. The tone shifts from mere survival toward bold plans for growth. Readers watch a colony and a mission find their stride at once.
journal-of-discourses-vol-04:
Volume Four, from 1857, was preached while a federal army marched on Utah. Johnston's troops drew near, and war talk filled the Salt Lake valley. The Saints readied to burn their homes and flee south.

Young's discourses breathe defiance and faith in the same breath here. Speakers vow to leave a scorched desert rather than yield their faith. Plans for flight, food stores, and guard duty share the pulpit's time. A people under siege hears its prophet plan and pray at once. The sermons catch a kingdom braced for its hardest test yet by arms. Trust in God and trust in Young stand as one here.
911-commission-report-2004:
Congress and President George W. Bush created the 9/11 Commission to explain the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The bipartisan panel, led by Thomas Kean and Lee Hamilton, held public hearings and reviewed millions of pages of records. Its final report appeared in July 2004 and became a bestseller, unusual for a government document.

The narrative traces the plot from its roots in Afghanistan to the morning of the attacks, and shows how agencies failed to share what they knew. The report blamed a failure of imagination across the government. Its proposals drove a major overhaul of American intelligence, including a new director over all the spy agencies. It stands as the main official history of the attacks.
monro-digest-justinian-vol1-1904:
Charles Henry Monro, a Cambridge lawyer, published the first volume of his English translation of Justinian's Digest in 1904. The Digest is the great anthology of Roman law, compiled for the Emperor Justinian in the sixth century from the writings of classical jurists. For centuries, English readers had needed Latin to use it.

Volume 1 opens the work: the nature of law and justice, the courts, and the standing of persons before the law. Monro translates with a lawyer's precision, keeping the jurists' terse style readable. The Digest became the foundation of legal systems across Europe, so an English version served scholars and barristers alike. Monro's volume began the task of making the Corpus Juris of Rome accessible in the language of the common-law world.
cia-0000007604:
Winter 1968 opened volume 12 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's journal written for its own staff. A heading in the issue reads like Ill Told Tales, tied to a book entry in its pages. The timing matters: early 1968 was the season of the Tet Offensive in Vietnam.

Book coverage inside a secret journal shows officers judging published work against private knowledge. Reviews and notes helped staff sort reliable accounts from weak ones. Historians value these issues because the writers assumed no outsider would read them. The declassified text thus catches the agency talking honestly among itself in wartime.
cia-0000008004:
Half of 1951 still lay ahead when CIA analysts forecast the rest of the year in Indochina. France was fighting the Viet Minh for control of Vietnam, and the war was going badly for Paris. American aid was growing, even though US troops were not yet involved.

Estimates like this one weighed French strength, Viet Minh gains, and China's role across the border. The writers had to judge a colonial war that Washington would later inherit. Their caution and errors both instruct, since the paper predates Dien Bien Phu by years. It is an early American attempt to read Vietnam's future.
cia-0000008704:
Two American pilots were sighted in An Thuy district, part of Haiphong, in a report dated January 1973. An Thuy lies near the port city's coast, in North Vietnam's northeast. The report arrived in the same month the Paris peace accords were signed.

Sightings filed at war's end held special weight, since they might describe men about to be freed or left behind. Officials compared such claims against the lists of prisoners Hanoi acknowledged. A mismatch kept a case open for years. This report preserves one of those end-of-war claims, with place and date, for the record that followed.
cia-0000009804:
A Viet Cong prisoner of war camp in Vinh Binh province, housing South Vietnamese and other prisoners, is described in a July 1971 report. The heading's list of who was held breaks off mid-word, after naming South Vietnamese and Viet Cong categories. Vinh Binh lies deep in the Mekong Delta.

Camps holding mixed populations show the southern war's tangled loyalties. Some inmates were government soldiers; others may have been the Viet Cong's own punished men. Untangling who was who fell to analysts reading reports like this one. The file preserves a Delta camp's population as reported, confusion included.
cia-0000012304:
Certain questions, the file's cut title suggests, occupy a Helms memo to the DIA director from November 1961. The memo closes a dense run of that autumn's Military Thought correspondence. Twelve months of such letters trace the operation's whole arc. They run from first contact to full industrial flow, each piece of Soviet writing matched to an American need.

The year's volume is the file's true subject: a spy case administered in full. The letters' rhythm never faltered across the seasons. For readers, this page is one count in the annual tally of the Cold War's most valuable penetration.
cia-0000012404:
Meeting number sixteen, London, May 5, 1961, closes the spring's intensive phase of the debriefings. Sixteen meetings in sixteen days: the opening blitz had no precedent. Soon Penkovsky would return to Moscow, where the work grew far more dangerous. There, contact ran through dead drops, signals, and rare meetings abroad. It could never match these long London sittings for volume or safety.

The record completes the first campaign of the case. Handlers closed the run with notebooks full and a source proven. For readers, the page marks the end of the beginning of a famous penetration.
cia-0000013604:
Nicaragua's political prospects over the next year or so are weighed in a CIA paper from September 1967. The Somoza family had ruled the country for three decades. Its grip ran through the National Guard, the treasury, and the family itself. The dynasty's corruption was its weakness, and the analysts weighed that weakness carefully against the opposition's small strength.

The paper judges the family's future at a settled moment in its long rule. Few then foresaw the revolution that would end it twelve years later. For readers, the paper shows the dynasty as Washington saw it then: durable, tainted, and watched.
cia-0000013904: American prisoners in two far apart provinces fill a CIA note dated November 2, 1967. One group was in Quang Binh Province in September 1965, in the north. Another mention points to Kontum, in the southern highlands. The note shows how a single file could join prisoner sightings across the whole length of Vietnam.
cia-0000015304: A letter to Samuel Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1958. It takes up points by Hynek and Lloyd, per the clipped title. Hynek was the Air Force's own astronomer on saucers. The mail shows agency men trading views with the few experts who knew the case files.
cia-0000022604: A dead American pilot was sighted in Hanoi, North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated in 1973. Hanoi was the capital, seat of the government that held American prisoners. A sighting there of a dead pilot carried weight for the final accounting of the war. Staff logged it in the year the living prisoners came home at last.
cia-0000028304: Stability of the present regime in Iran is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1958. The present regime meant the Shah's government, five years after the coup that secured it. Stability papers asked how deep a ruler's support ran and where the cracks might open. For Iran the question would return with far greater force twenty years later.
cia-0000042704:
President Cristiani issued a statement on the murder investigation, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. Alfredo Cristiani was El Salvador's president during the war's last years. His government stood accused by critics of shielding the killers.

Inside, the president's own words on the investigation are set down. A head of state under fire chooses each such word with great care. The file preserves the official promise of an inquiry. Readers can weigh that promise against the slow course the case then took, as soldiers were named, held, and tried over the years that followed.
cia-0000037104: Disbursements for travel and other expenses fill a CIA record dated November 5, 1942, naming Cook, Phenix, Osborne, Tyler, Rado, and others. The page comes from the OSS, the wartime office that stood behind the later CIA. It sets out payments name by name in the plain hand of a ledger keeper. Wartime secret work still ran on vouchers and receipts, and pages like this one kept the young office's spending in order.
cia-0000049004: Many Salvadoran military officers were pleased by the assassination of leaders of the revolutionary movement, and a CIA item dated November 1, 1980, records their reaction. The item is a cold one: satisfaction at murder, noted in plain bureaucratic words. It survives among the Truth Commission files as evidence of the climate inside the armed forces.
cia-0000049104: Victor Manuel Santos Marinez is the named subject of a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. The series is full of such single-name files, each a person caught in the war's paperwork. What the system knew about him sits in the document, behind a title that gives nothing else away.
cia-0000049404: The Election Outlook in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049404, dated May 5, 1982. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper looks ahead to a Salvadoran election. It is a brief declassified forecast whose title states its aim, companion in spirit to the agency's other Salvadoran election outlook from two years later.
cia-0000098304: Chinese Communist short-range military intentions, with intentions misspelled in the heading, are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098304, dated June 4, 1962. The title limits its scope to the short range. Readers find a brief declassified intentions paper from China reporting, its spelling flaw preserved in the catalog beside its more polished neighbors.
arxiv-2606-07804: An arXiv research paper from 2026, this manuscript presents new work. The title's topic is Quantum-Inspired Reinforcement Learning for Low-Latency Intrusion Detection in V2X and Internet-of-Vehicles Networks. The paper works the ground of artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. It places a new research result before the scientific community.
arxiv-2606-08004: An arXiv research paper from 2026, this manuscript presents new work. The subject matter, per the title, is Tracking metastable phases by complex Lee-Yang zeros. The paper lives in science and technology, careful study of how the natural and built world works. The manuscript's findings join the public body of research.
arxiv-2606-08204: New on arXiv in 2026, this manuscript brings a fresh research result. The title sets the topic as Neural Field Tokenizations with Hierarchy and Spatial Locality Priors. The subject area is artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. It places a new research result before the scientific community.
arxiv-2606-08404: Issued on arXiv in 2026, this manuscript reports a new line of work. The title tells readers the subject is Geometry-Driven Poisson Flow Model of Cortical Manifolds. The field in play is mathematics: the study of numbers, shapes, patterns, and logical proof. It records a new contribution to human knowledge.
