plos-pone-0004804: Bt cotton targets caterpillars, but what about aphids? Lawo and colleagues tested whether Indian Bt cotton varieties harm cotton aphids or their predators. They found no effect on aphid performance. The result supports Bt cotton's safety for non-target insects in the field.
plos-pone-0005404: TRPM8 is the cold-sensing ion channel, and polyphosphate tunes it. Zakharian and team show inorganic polyphosphate tunes TRPM8 channel function. The ancient polymer controls a modern sensor. Cold detection with a phosphate dial, adjustable by energy use, a new control layer for temperature sensation.
plos-pone-0005504: Sepsis floods the body with norepinephrine, worsening swelling. Miksa and team showed the alpha-2A-adrenoceptor drives swelling and organ injury in septic rats. The sensor is a healing target. Stress hormones fueling the septic fire, sensor by sensor, and blocking this sensor could calm septic swelling.
plos-pone-0005604: Mast cells tune allergic effects by internalizing sensors. Molfetta and team showed lipid-raft-dependent ubiquitination controls Fc-epsilon-RI endocytosis. The process controls allergy signal. Taking allergy sensors off the air via ubiquitin, cell biology of allergic control, with new angles on mast-cell control.
plos-pone-0005704: Kidney scarring involves inborn immune sensors. Leemans and team showed TLR2 drives swelling and fibrosis during progressive renal injury. The sensor is a healing target. Inborn defense scarring the kidney, sensor by sensor, nephrology with an immune angle, suggesting blocking TLR2 to save kidneys.
plos-pone-0005804: An joint pain drug may help kill cancer. Marchetti and team showed sulindac lifts killing of with oxygen stressed cancer cells. The NSAID's cancer-blocking promise grows. Reusing anti-inflammatories against cancer, in vitro, COX blocking's cancer angle, colon polyp blocking's lead, oxygen stress as a healing lever.
plos-pone-0006504: Itch chemical's newest receptor brakes blood starters. Petit-Bertron and team found H4 itch chemical receptors halt growth in blood starter cells. The brake, in marrow — blood's pause button, mapped, in mouse and human cells. Bone marrow home, H4R in focus: cell cycle arrest.
plos-pone-0006604: Cell antennas tune signals in fat rafts. Fallahi-Sichani and Linderman modeled GPCR signals in lipid rafts. Pairing shapes the message — docks' raft rules, modeled, for the largest receptor family. G-proteins woken, dimers weighed: ligands steer pairing, math study, purpose probed.
plos-pone-0009404: Dendritic cells are the immune system's scouts, sounding the alarm that wakes up the body's defenses. This paper reads the full gene-activity patterns of these cells as they are activated or calmed. The resulting inflammatory signatures give doctors a molecular fingerprint of immune arousal — useful for spotting when vaccines work, infections rage, or the immune system misfires.
plos-pone-0009504: Hepatitis C infects 200 million people and usually becomes a lifelong liver infection. This paper shows that a sugar-binding protein called galectin-9, released by liver immune cells, helps regulate T cell attacks during the infection. The finding maps a key control lever in the immune battle — one that could be tuned to help patients clear the virus.
plos-pone-0009604: Silicosis — lung scarring from inhaled silica dust — remains untreatable. This mouse study examines the role of RAGE, a receptor that senses tissue damage, in the disease. The paper tests whether blocking this alarm receptor could slow the lung's self-destruction.
plos-pone-0010404: Many depressed patients don't respond to antidepressants, and there was no good animal model of that resistance. This study combines chronic stress with a high-fat diet in mice to create one. The paper offers a tool for studying treatment-resistant depression.
plos-pone-0010504: Insulin's effects could be prolonged by blocking the enzyme that destroys it. This study designs inhibitors of insulin-degrading enzyme and tests their effects on insulin activity. The paper explores a new angle on diabetes therapy that works with the body's own hormone.
plos-pone-0010604: Single-letter protein changes cause devastating lamin diseases. This study develops antibodies that specifically recognize two disease mutants, R453W and R482W. The paper provides precise tools for studying laminopathies. The tools let scientists watch mutant proteins misbehave in cells.
plos-pone-0010704: Cells fold proteins with a machine called CCT. This study shows two of its subunits are essential for building cilia in Tetrahymena. The paper links protein folding to cellular antennae. The finding connects protein chaperones to cilia and cellular motility.
plos-pone-0010804: Autistic adults may read fleeting fearful faces differently at the brain level. This study scans amygdala responses to barely visible anxious faces in adults with autism spectrum disorders. The paper offers preliminary insights. The findings probe how social-emotional wiring differs in ASD.
plos-pone-0010904: A single rhodopsin typo, Q344ter, causes inherited blindness. This mouse study shows the mutant protein mislocalizes in photoreceptors yet remains catalytically active. The paper unravels a subtle disease mechanism. The model guides future retinal therapies. The active-but-lost protein poisons vision.
plos-pone-0011004: In cystic fibrosis, lung macrophages fan the flames. This study shows switching off the CFTR gene makes these immune cells angry and boosts a protein called caveolin-1. The paper reveals a cell-level mechanism. The finding suggests new ways to calm CF lungs.
plos-pone-0011104: Yeast cells sense stress through clustered surface sentinels. This single-molecule atomic force microscopy study reveals Wsc1 sensors clustering in the yeast plasma membrane. The paper visualizes nanoscale organization. The finding informs cell-signaling research. The organization shows how cells feel their surroundings.
plos-pone-0011204: Pig sperm must dock their acrosomes to fertilize. This study demonstrates stable acrosome docking to the plasma membrane during sperm activation in the oviduct. The paper reveals a key fertilization step. The finding informs animal breeding. The step is a target for contraception.
plos-pone-0011304: An immune gene regulator moonlights in HIV assembly. This study shows the class II transactivator (CIITA) enhances cytoplasmic processing of the HIV-1 Pr55Gag protein. The paper reveals a viral-assembly twist. The finding informs HIV research. The informed research hunts new drug targets.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1304:
Harrison wrote to Stimson again on 17 July 1945, the day Potsdam opened. The acting chairman of the Interim Committee kept the war secretary supplied as the atomic news ripened. Their exchange ran beside the public talks like a second, hidden summit.

Stimson, at Potsdam, was the one man there who carried the whole atomic secret for the American side. Harrison's notes fed him the home end of that file: test word, committee views, and pending choices. This message is one link in that channel. It shows the bomb's policy being handled in quiet notes while the conference made its noise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1404:
Caffery cabled the acting secretary of state again on 7 August 1945, the day after his cluster of Paris reports. The Potsdam Conference had closed five days earlier. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

The week after a summit is when its choices land on the desks of ambassadors, who must explain them to the governments they live among. Caffery's steady cables show that landing in France. Readers can watch the post-conference work unfold: questions from Paris, answers from the embassy, reports to Washington. It is less grand than the summit itself, and closer to how the settlement was actually carried into the world.
frus-1945-50-intel-d104:
Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 1, dated 19 February 1946, is the new body's first numbered order. The CIG had been created by the president's directive four weeks earlier. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

First directives set a body's working habits: who may task it, what it may collect, and how its products reach the departments. Directive No. 1 turned the January compromise into daily practice. Readers should read it as the CIG's birth certificate in operational form. Everything the group later became, a true central agency in embryo, starts from the authorities and limits written here, under its first director, Sidney Souers.
frus-1945-50-intel-d204:
A memorandum dated 23 January 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division of the Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). Readers meet it as document 204 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d304:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Forrestal reached Acting Secretary of State Lovett on 13 October 1948. It is document 304 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

A letter fixed a position in a way a phone call never could: dated, signed, and filed for both sides to cite later. Its worth now is the voice: a chief stating his case as he wished it to be read. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d404:
James Lay, acting executive secretary of the National Security Council, sent a memo to the Council itself on 14 December 1949. The paper is document 404 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Council joined the President with his top foreign and defense aides. Its executive secretary handled the flow of papers that set up each meeting and recorded each choice. A memo from that office to the Council shows the staff machine behind Cold War choices at the highest level. Lay later held the secretary's post in full, a sign of the trust this staff work earned.
frus-1861-d104:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 October 1861. The letter is document 104 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Lyons's last October note in the file keeps the formal round intact. The two governments had learned to argue without breaking. That habit, built letter by letter, would soon be tested harder than either man yet knew. That habit of formal calm would soon face the Trent, the hardest test of the war's first year. The hardest test found the habit strong, which is why the tie survived it.
frus-1861-d204:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Eduard de Stoeckl on 7 September 1861. De Stoeckl was the Russian minister in Washington. The letter is document 204 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

De Stoeckl had served in Washington for years and knew its ways well. Seward's letter to him worked the home end of the Russian tie. Between them, the two men kept the warmest link the Union had in Europe running smoothly. De Stoeckl's long service made him half an insider in the capital he served. Half an insider is a rare post for a foreign envoy, and he filled it well.
frus-1861-d304:
Seward's incoming mail for 27 July 1861 held a dispatch from Mr. Turpin. The printed record keeps it as Document 304 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d104:
17 July 1862 is the date on a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 104 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d204:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 13 January 1862, in a note printed as Document 204 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, handled the American war from the legation there.

Mid-January found both governments glad to leave the Trent quarrel behind, yet watchful. The Union blockade of Southern ports and British trade losses from it promised fresh disputes. Short formal notes like this one were the everyday tools for managing those disputes before they hardened, and the file holds many from this winter. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d304:
Dated 18 August 1862, Document 304 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

The letter went out eleven days before the second battle of Bull Run, in the last stretch of the summer's buildup. Seward's tone in this period stayed formal and assured, whatever the news. That practiced calm was policy: envoys abroad took their cue from the Secretary's voice, and foreign governments read it as a measure of Union confidence. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d404:
One day after his previous order, on 24 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The note is Document 404 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress with the annual message.

Back-to-back instructions usually meant fast-moving news or a point Seward wanted stressed without delay. In June 1862 the fighting in Virginia and the allied quarrel in Mexico both pressed on Spanish policy. Small as it is, the dispatch shows how closely Washington managed its Madrid post. Much of Civil War diplomacy was done this way, in brief, frequent letters rather than grand notes.
frus-1862-d504:
On 4 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. It is Document 504 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

June opened with the armies facing each other before Richmond and the war's outcome once again in doubt. Seward's orders that month mixed resolve with careful answers to specific Dutch questions about ports and shipping. The Netherlands file in the volume is long because both sides wrote often and on small matters as well as large. An instruction of this kind is best read as maintenance: keeping a friendly neutrality in good repair while the great battles were decided elsewhere.
frus-1862-d604:
Admiral Jurien de la Gravière, the French naval commander in the Mexican expedition, wrote this letter to Spain's General Prim on 20 March 1862. It is Document 604 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, annexed to Prim's own despatch.

An annex travels with the document that encloses it. So a French admiral's letter survives here inside a Spanish general's report. The report is printed in an American volume. The layering is the point: the allied commanders in Mexico were already at odds that March, and their private exchanges show it. For the reader, the letter is a small, sharp piece of the coalition's breakup, preserved through three governments' paperwork.
frus-1862-d704:
Charles N. Riotte sent this dispatch from Costa Rica to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 September 1862. Riotte was the American minister there. The letter is document 704 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

By the fall of 1862 Riotte had a year's worth of Central American ground to report on. His mail dealt with the republics' affairs, the transit trade, and the claims of Americans in the region. Letters like this one formed Washington's best source on a part of the world it cared about chiefly for the road between the seas. The record still shows that care, one dispatch at a time.
frus-1863p1-d104:
On 2 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the eighth of twelve to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 104 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Late in a long batch, a writer turns to the smaller heads of a brief: the points that need a word but not a speech. Seward's eighth sheet of the day is of that kind, by its place in the row. Together the twelve gave Adams a full kit for the spring's talks in London. This letter is one tool in that kit, plain and to its point.
frus-1863p1-d204:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 19 May 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 204 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d304:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 5 October 1863. The letter is document 304 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. By then the British government had moved to hold the Confederate rams, and the sharpest crisis of the year was cooling. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d404: On 28 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 404 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d504:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 11 May 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d604:
Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons took up his pen on 7 August 1863 and wrote to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020004:
Tomoko Ishino, Kazuhiko Yano, Yasuo Chinzei, and their group traced a step in malaria infection for PLOS Biology in 2004. After a mosquito bite, malaria parasites travel to the liver. A sheet of cells lines the liver's blood vessels, and the parasites must cross it to reach liver cells.

The team found that the parasites need a cell-passage skill to make that crossing. They actively move through cells rather than slipping between them. Blocking that skill could, in theory, stop infection before the liver stage takes hold. The paper matters because the liver stage is a brief, quiet window. A drug or vaccine that works there could prevent illness outright.
plos-pbio-0020104:
Zhixin Xie, Lisa K. Johansen, Adam M. Gustafson, and a large team mapped small RNA pathways in plants for PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use small RNAs to silence genes, fight viruses, and control growth. The team sorted the many small RNAs of the model plant Arabidopsis and traced how they are made.

They found that the pathways branch more than expected, with distinct sets of small RNAs doing distinct jobs. Some guard the genome against jumping genes, while others fine-tune growth genes. A full catalog of these RNAs gives plant science a working map. It also informs crop work, since the same pathways shape traits like yield and disease resistance.
plos-pbio-0020304:
Dennis R. Harris, Masashi Tanaka, Sergei V. Saveliev, and their team studied a radiation-proof bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Deinococcus radiodurans survives doses of radiation that shatter its genome into hundreds of pieces, then rebuilds it. The authors focus on a protein called DdrA that appears after damage.

DdrA guards the broken ends of DNA, keeping them from being chewed away before repair starts. That protection buys time for the cell's rebuilding tools. The bacterium's tricks are of keen interest for cleaning up radioactive waste and for understanding DNA repair in general. Each named part, like DdrA, brings the full system closer to view.
plos-pone-0000104:
Michael A. Pickart, Eric W. Klee, Aubrey L. Nielsen, and a large team built a genetics toolkit in PLOS ONE in 2006. The secretome is the set of proteins a cell secretes, its outward messages and tools. Many of their jobs were unknown. The team's framework knocks down these genes one by one in vertebrate embryos to reveal their roles.

Reverse genetics starts from the gene and asks what breaks without it. Applied at genome scale to secreted proteins, it promises a catalog of what our cells say to each other. Secreted proteins are prime drug targets, since they can be reached outside the cell. A map of their functions is thus both basic biology and a drug hunter's chart.
plos-pone-0000204:
Nikolas Nikolaidis, Dimitra Chalkia, D. Neil Watkins, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It argues for the ancient origin of a group of developmental genes the authors call DANGER, described as a new developmental superfamily. These genes are involved in how embryos build their bodies.

Tracing a gene family to an ancient origin changes when scientists think its roles began. The authors compare sequences across species to date the family. If the superfamily is as old as they argue, its genes were part of the toolkit of very early animals, not a later addition.
plos-pone-0000304:
Xavier Dramard, Thierry Heidmann, and Silke Jensen published this genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The I-factor is a LINE retrotransposon, a jumping gene in fruit flies that can cause sterility when it runs loose. The authors describe natural epigenetic protection against it: fragments left by ancestral invasions of the element silence the modern copies.

The genome, in effect, keeps souvenirs of old invasions that vaccinate it against new ones. The authors document that protection in Drosophila. The work is a neat case of an arms race written into DNA, where the host's defense is built from the invader's own remains.
plos-pone-0000404:
Remus Oşan and colleagues applied a mathematical technique to brain data in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Neural networks in the brain encode information in patterns spread across many cells, and those patterns are hard to read from raw recordings. The team used subspace projection methods to classify and display these network-level encoding patterns.

Subspace projection simplifies high-dimensional data by finding the directions that carry the real signal. Applied to neural activity, it can sort patterns by what they represent and show them in pictures a human can grasp. Better readouts of population activity serve research on memory, movement, and brain-computer interfaces, where decoding many cells at once is the whole problem.
plos-pone-0000504:
Cindy Voisine and colleagues used a millimeter-long worm to screen for Huntington's disease drugs, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is a fatal inherited brain disease with no cure. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans can be engineered to carry the disease's defect, and the team used it for identification of potential therapeutic drugs.

Worms are cheap, fast, and easy to dose, so thousands of compounds can be tested in weeks. Hits from a worm screen still face a long road through mouse and human testing, but the screen widens the funnel's mouth. The study is an example of model-organism drug discovery aimed at a disease that human trials alone cannot explore quickly.
plos-pone-0000604:
Elena M. Boggio and colleagues watched a signaling enzyme light up in two cell compartments at once after visual input, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. ERK is an enzyme that relays activity signals inside neurons. The team showed that visual stimulation activates ERK in two parts of rat cortical neurons. ERK rose in the synaptic compartment and in the somatic compartment. Both responses ran on the same timetable.

Parallel timing suggests the synapse and the nucleus-bound machinery are coordinated when the visual system adapts to input. ERK activation is a step in plasticity, the process by which seeing reshapes the seeing brain. Rat visual cortex is a standard model for how experience tunes sensory systems early in life.
plos-pone-0000704:
Jeroen R. P. M. Strating, Gerrit Bouw, Theo G. M. Hafmans and colleagues compared two members of a protein transport family, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The p24 family is thought to help move proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, the cell's shipping and sorting stations. A subset of p24 proteins rises when frog pituitary cells are activated to produce more hormone.

The title previews a contrast: p24 alpha and p24 delta have disparate effects on secretory protein transport and processing. Two relatives pulling differently complicates any simple family story. For cell biologists, sorting out who does what in the early secretory pathway underpins everything cells export, from hormones to antibodies.
plos-pone-0000804:
Tsunglin Liu, Thales Papagiannakopoulos, Kathy Puskar and colleagues searched living tissue data for the fingerprint of microRNAs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are short non-coding transcripts, about 21 nucleotides long, capable of regulating gene expression. The best-studied mechanism has a microRNA binding its target messenger RNA, after which translation is inhibited and the message may be destroyed.

If microRNAs act in vivo, sets of real mRNAs should carry a detectable signal of that action, in their sequences or levels. The team reports detecting such a signal in an in vivo expression set. Confirming lab mechanisms in whole organisms tells researchers microRNA rules learned in dishes still govern living systems.
plos-pone-0000904:
Eriikka Heikkinen, Teemu Kallonen, Lilli Saarinen and colleagues compared whooping cough germs across Finland, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough and has returned in many countries. Finland has used the whole cell vaccine for more than fifty years, yet cases rose again.

The team compared genomes of Finnish strains and report steady gene loss over time. A germ that sheds genes while a vaccine presses on it raises hard questions about adaptation. Their comparison helps health officials judge whether vaccines still match the germ in circulation. It also shows evolution at work inside a single country.
plos-pone-0001004:
Samantha Morris, Alexandra Almeida, Hideaki Tanaka and colleagues showed how a factor called Tsukushi tunes embryo signals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In early frog development, the middle germ layer forms when lower cells signal to cells above them. Whole body layers arise from such local conversations.

Tsukushi modulates three signal families at once: Xnr2, FGF and BMP. Tuning several signals together can set the borders of the germ layers with precision. The work was done in Xenopus, the standard frog for embryo studies. A single factor touching three pathways is a reminder that embryo signals form a web, not separate wires.
plos-pone-0001104:
Jeffrey Petrella, Steven Prince, Lihong Wang and colleagues tested a brain signal's power to predict decline in mild cognitive impairment, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Healthy people deactivate a region called the posteromedial cortex during many tasks. Brain imaging had suggested that this deactivation during memory tasks is impaired in Alzheimer's disease.

Mild cognitive impairment sits between normal aging and Alzheimer's. The team assess the prognostic value of posteromedial deactivation in such patients: does a weaker signal foresee worse decline. A predictor at this stage would help families plan and trials recruit the right patients. Imaging markers are plentiful; prognostic proof is the rare part.
plos-pone-0001204:
When immune cells meet, they form a structured contact zone called the immunological synapse. Oded Rechavi and colleagues report a surprising event at that zone in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. An oncogenic protein, H-Ras, transfers from one cell to another there. The synapse is known for regions of membrane fusion and exchanges of membrane fragments between the cells.

The authors show that the cancer-associated form of H-Ras moves between cells at the synapse. A growth-promoting protein passing hand to hand could change how the receiving cell behaves. The finding adds a new route by which signals, healthy or harmful, spread through the immune system.
plos-pone-0001304:
Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep caused by prions, infectious proteins. Gillian McGovern and Martin Jeffrey describe the disease's specific pathology in sheep lymphoid tissues, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Prion diseases often cause accumulation of the disease-associated prion protein in the lymphoreticular system, the network of immune tissues.

The protein builds up in association with follicular dendritic cells and tingible body macrophages in secondary lymphoid organs. Mapping exactly where it accumulates helps diagnose scrapie from tissue samples, which matters for flock surveillance. The lymphoid pattern also hints at how prions spread through the body before reaching the brain.
plos-pone-0001404:
Sheena Lee and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on spinal muscular atrophy, a gene based ill that weakens muscle. In this disease, one gene is lost, but a near twin gene gives weak backup. The protein's full job was still not clear. The team read gene use across the genome in a model of the disease.

Their broad scan named sets of genes whose use shifts when the key protein is low. Those shifts point to paths that may drive the muscle loss. They also give a list of fresh drug targets to test. The work moves from one lost gene to the wider web it disturbs.
plos-pone-0001504:
Mehmet Somel and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on diet and gene use in humans and chimps. The human diet strays far from that of our close primate kin. What that stray means for gene gaps was unknown. The team fed lab mice diets in the style of human or chimp food.

Gene use in the mice shifted with diet. Some shifts copied the known gaps between human and chimp gene use. That hints diet alone can drive part of the species gap. It warns that gene comparisons must weigh food and lab life. It also gives a tool to test diet effects in a strict way.
plos-pone-0001604:
Dean Smith, Julie Rosenheimer, and Ronald Kalil published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on ion channels in young rat nerve stem cells. These channels help set how cells fire, and they matter for growth and cell division. No full account of them existed for nerve stem cells from the rat brain's growth zone. The team recorded the currents cell by cell.

They chart two main channel types and how each opens and shuts. The chart is a base map for how these stem cells talk in bursts. It helps labs tell stem cells from their mature kin by their currents. It may also hint at how channel faults skew brain growth.
plos-pone-0001704:
Geraldine A. Wright, Sonya M. Kottcamp, and Mitchell G. A. Thomson studied how honeybees judge odors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals use smells to tell mates, kin, and food apart, even though natural odor amounts vary a lot. Generalization, treating two different stimuli as alike, helps an animal decide that a changed smell still means the same thing.

The authors show that generalization is what lets bees stay sensitive to complex odor features despite that variation. The full text gives the training tests, the odor blends, and the bees' choices. The work explains a puzzle in animal senses. A nose can be both finely tuned and tolerant of noise, a balance that robot sensors still struggle to copy.
plos-pone-0001804:
Mustafa Raoof, Haq Nawaz, Rabeeya Nusrat, and their co-authors surveyed sedative use in Pakistan in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Benzodiazepines are prescribed too freely in Pakistan and are available over the counter without prescription, a major public health problem. Data on how much people knew about these drugs, and how much they used them, was limited.

Their one-time survey covered healthy volunteers and clinic patients visiting a large care hospital. The full text gives how much people knew, the usage rates, and where people got the drugs. Benzodiazepines are habit forming, so measuring casual use and low awareness gives health chiefs the baseline they need to tighten supply and warn the public.
plos-pone-0001904:
Wassim Chehab and co-authors split apart two plant defense signals in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When pests or germs attack, plants fire back with chemical defenses. Two groups of signals drive much of that response. One is the jasmonates, and the other is six-carbon aldehydes, both made from fats in the leaf by two rival branches of one pathway.

Because the branches compete, their roles are hard to untangle. The team used plants in which one branch or the other was changed, to see what each signal group does on its own. Clear roles for each signal help crop science breed or treat plants that resist pests with fewer sprays.
plos-pone-0002004:
Elizabeth Clement and co-authors recorded brain waves that cycle like sleep under anesthesia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Sleep and general anesthesia both bring unconsciousness and share some brain steps. But sleep is not flat: it cycles between active REM sleep and quiet sleep. Whether anesthesia shows like cycles was less clear.

Under urethane anesthesia, a standard lab drug, the team recorded spontaneous shifts of brain state. As the title states, the brain showed cyclic, sleep-like alternations. If an anesthetized brain still cycles, depth of anesthesia may rise and fall on its own. That fact matters for both brain science and surgery.
plos-pone-0002104:
Timur Akchurin and co-authors tracked the birth and death of bone-eating cells in long-term culture, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Osteoclasts are the cells that resorb bone. They contribute to degenerative, metabolic, and neoplastic bone diseases, which often show lasting changes in the bone's local setting. How a population of these cells rises and falls over time was not well charted.

The team aimed to investigate the dynamics of osteoclast formation and death in cultures kept for the long term. They report complex dynamics, not a simple rise and fade. Bone drugs act on these very dynamics.
plos-pone-0002204:
Kwasi Torpey, Mushota Kabaso, Liya Mutale, and co-authors described a staffing fix for HIV care in Zambia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Clinics offering antiretroviral therapy, the drugs that keep HIV in check, face severe staff shortages. Good adherence counseling helps patients take their drugs on schedule, but nurses and doctors have little time for it.

The Zambia Prevention, Care and Treatment Partnership trained community volunteers as adherence support workers at health facilities. These lay workers took on counseling and follow-up tasks. The program shows how care can be shared more widely, so scarce clinical staff can focus on the work only they can do.
plos-pone-0002304:
Heather Ishak, John Dumbacher, Nancy Anderson, and co-authors surveyed blood parasites in owls, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. All three subspecies of the Spotted Owl are threatened by habitat loss and by the spread of the Barred Owl into their range. One unexamined threat was whether Barred Owls carry blood parasites that could infect Spotted Owls.

The team screened owls for blood parasites and compared what each species carries. If the invading Barred Owl brings new parasites, contact between the two could add disease pressure to a bird already losing ground. Surveys like this one tell conservation teams whether disease belongs on the threat list.
plos-pone-0002404:
Led by Iwai, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Yoshiko Iwai, Hiroaki Hemmi, Olga Mizenina, and others. Its subject is an IFN-γ-IL-18 Signaling Loop Accelerates Memory CD8 + T Cell Proliferation. Rapid proliferation is one of the important features of memory CD8 + T cells, ensuring rapid clearance of reinfection.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002504:
Research by Hemminki and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Kari Hemminki, Asta Försti, Justo Lorenzo Bermejo, and others. Its subject is the ‘Common Disease-Common Variant’ Hypothesis and Familial Risks. The recent large genotyping studies have identified a new repertoire of disease susceptibility loci of unknown function.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002604:
Bunnell and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Tina M. Bunnell, Michele A. Jaeger, Daniel P. Fitzsimons, and others. Its subject is destabilization of the Dystrophin-Glycoprotein Complex without Functional Deficits in α-Dystrobrevin Null Muscle. α-Dystrobrevin is a component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) and is thought to have both structural and signaling roles in skeletal muscle.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002704:
Research from Eva Madi Riising and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers the polycomb repressive complex 2 is a potential target of SUMO modifications. The catalog record names Eva Madi Riising first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) functions as a transcriptional repressor through a mechanism that involves methylation of Histone H3 at lysine 27. The authors add a further point. The PRC2 complex activity is essential for cellular proliferation, development, and cell fate decisions. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002804:
Work by Sigeng Chen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with dopamine inhibits mitochondrial motility in hippocampal neurons. Authorship is credited in the record to Sigeng Chen and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The trafficking of mitochondria within neurons is a highly regulated process. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002904:
Jijun Hao, Marie Daleo, Clare Murphy and co-authors tested a small drug called dorsomorphin in stem cells in 2008. Embryonic stem cells can become any tissue type, which makes them a hopeful source for repair medicine. Guiding them into one chosen type, such as heart muscle, needs precise signals.

Dorsomorphin selectively blocks BMP signaling, one of those growth signals. In PLOS ONE the team reports that blocking BMP this way promotes cardiomyogenesis, the making of heart muscle cells, in embryonic stem cells. That gives labs a simple chemical tool for steering stem cells toward the heart.
plos-pone-0003004:
Sven Hoffmann and Michael Falkenstein compared two ways to clean eye blink artifacts from EEG in 2008. Blinks swamp the brain signals that electroencephalograms record. The study investigated what impact blinks leave behind after correction by a regression method and by independent component analysis.

The two prominent methods are named EMCP for the regression approach and ICA for the component approach. Published in PLOS ONE, a head-to-head check on residual impact helps labs pick a cleaning method with evidence. Clean EEG matters for any study reading thought or perception from scalp signals. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003104:
Adam de Smith, Robin Walters, Lachlan Coin and co-authors studied small deletion variants in human DNA in 2008. Copy number variants contribute greatly to human genomic variation, with over 5,000 loci reported covering more than 18 percent of the genome. Little was known about the origin and stability of variants of different sizes.

Small deletions have stable breakpoints commonly associated with Alu elements, repeated DNA sequences, the title reports. Stable break points suggest these variants arise and persist in orderly ways. Published in PLOS ONE, the work helps interpret the deletions found in patient genome scans.
plos-pone-0003204:
Monika Madan and Salomon Amar link an immune sensor to atherosclerosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Accumulating evidence implicates a fundamental link between the immune system and atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind most heart attacks. Toll-like receptors are principal sensors of the innate immune system. The team report an assessment of the role of the TLR2 pathway in atherosclerosis linked with a high-fat diet and pathogens.

They present proteomic findings, a broad survey of proteins, to support that role. Readers see diet, infection and immunity drawn into one artery story. The work suggests immune sensors could be targets in heart disease prevention.
plos-pone-0003304:
Bindu Chandrasekharan, Vanitha Bala, Vasantha L. Kolachala and colleagues delete a neuropeptide gene in a colitis model in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Neurogenic inflammation plays a major role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease. The team examined the role of neuropeptide Y and neuronal nitric oxide synthase in shaping colitis. Colitis was induced by giving dextran sodium sulphate.

The title reports that targeted deletion of neuropeptide Y modulates experimental colitis. Readers see gut nerves treated as active players in bowel inflammation, not bystanders. Nerve signals may offer drug angles apart from calming the immune system alone.
plos-pone-0007404: Stone tools can trace ancient human migrations where fossils are silent. This study treated Acheulean handaxes — the teardrop-shaped tools made for over a million years — like biological traits, mapping their shapes across continents to rebuild how early hominins spread. The analysis shows that tool-making traditions carry a family-tree signal, letting archaeologists read ancient dispersals from the stones themselves.
plos-pone-0007504: More than 30 bat species migrate, yet almost no one had asked how migration evolved in bats. Studying the largest bat family, the researchers found evidence that migration arose independently multiple times rather than once. The repeated invention of the same lifestyle points to strong pressures pushing bats to travel.
plos-pone-0007604: Cells destroy misfolded proteins through a disposal system, and this study dissected a helper protein called Usa1 that tags targets for destruction. Usa1 works through two separate domains to help attach the ubiquitin disposal label. The finding illuminates a quality-control system whose failure underlies neurodegenerative disease.
plos-pone-0007704: Stress hormones act on the brain's glucocorticoid receptors, and this study shows their gene-switching effects in the dentate gyrus raise anxiety-like behavior in mice. The region-specific finding pinpoints where in the hippocampus stress writes its anxious signature.
plos-pone-0007804: Staph abscesses resist many treatments, but nitric oxide — a natural antimicrobial — kills the bacteria if it can be delivered. This study packaged NO into nanoparticles and cured staph abscesses in mice. The particle delivery solves the gas's Achilles' heel: it vanishes too fast to work alone.
plos-pone-0007904: Synovial sarcoma carries a signature fusion gene, SYT-SSX1, but it only transforms certain cells. This study showed the epigenetic state of mesenchymal stem cells decides whether the fusion gene can reprogram them. The finding explains why the same mutation is harmless in most tissues and deadly in a few.
plos-pone-0008004: A protein that sculpts DNA has favorite landing spots. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Manabe and colleagues hunted for the DNA sequences gripped by HMGA1a, a protein that bends the genome's shape to control genes. It prefers stretches rich in A and T, the DNA letters, and touches many normal processes from growth to immunity. The new catalog of candidate binding sites maps where this architectural protein does its shaping work.
plos-pone-0008104: Chemotherapy poisons topoisomerases — the enzymes that untangle DNA. This study found the E3 ubiquitin ligase Bmi1/Ring1A controls the destruction of poisoned Top2α complexes. The degradation pathway is a potential new drug target for making chemo work better.
plos-pone-0008204: Spinal muscular atrophy starves motor neurons of the SMN protein. This study used adenoviral vectors carrying antisense sequences in U7 RNAs to restore full-length SMN. The gene-therapy approach coaxes the backup gene SMN2 into making the real thing.
plos-pone-0008304: Platelet clotting is tuned by a phosphatase. This 2009 study showed the catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 1 gamma regulates thrombin-induced platelet integrin function. Fine-tuning this enzyme could yield anti-clotting drugs with fewer bleeding risks.
plos-pone-0008404: Ovarian tumors were triggered by deleting two guardians. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Quinn's team knocked out Brca1 and p53 in mouse ovaries, inducing leiomyosarcomas. Inherited BRCA1 mutations drive many ovarian cancers. The double-knockout model mirrors the human disease. The mice give a testbed for therapies.
plos-pone-0008504: Denials were found hiding real infections. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Cachay's team showed HIV-positive men who deny risk behavior still carry asymptomatic anorectal STIs. CDC screening hinges on self-report. The hidden infections argue for routine testing. The finding changes screening practice.
plos-pone-0008604: Breast cancer's drug resistance got a double key. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Crawford's team showed co-blocking BCL-W and BCL2 restores antiestrogen sensitivity via BECN1, triggering autophagy-linked necrosis. The anti-death duo's role was decoded. The double hit kills resistant cells. The combo suggests new therapy.
plos-pone-0008704: Kinase targets got a proteomic dragnet. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Amano's team built a proteomic screen for protein kinase substrates like Rho-kinase. The signaling enzymes' hit lists needed mapping. The dragnet's catches were decoded. The screen accelerates pathway mapping.
plos-pone-0008804: A stomach germ was found shielding against TB. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Perry's team showed Helicobacter pylori infection protects against tuberculosis. The lifelong stomach resident's immune tweak was mapped. The shield reveals microbial diplomacy.
plos-pone-0008904: A plant defense gene got a messenger job. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Meier's team showed Arabidopsis WAKL10 is a functional guanylyl cyclase co-expressed with defense genes. The cGMP link was mapped. The job reveals plant immunity.
plos-pone-0009004: Two-tongue kids got a talk edge. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Siegal's team found two-tongue kids read conversations better. The 3-to-6 crowd's talk smarts were tested in four languages. The edge feeds language science. The win shows bilingual brains tune in.
plos-pone-0009104: Parkinson's got a blood-flag candidate. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Shehadeh's team flagged SRRM2 blood signs in Parkinson's. The flag was mapped in patients. The flag may aid early spotting. The flag surfaced in a splicing-wide screen.
plos-pone-0009204: Mouse eggs got a chemo-survival recipe. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kujjo's team boosted oocyte survival after chemo or aging by targeting Bax and Rad51. The fertility-preserving trick was mapped. The recipe suggests fertility care.
plos-pone-0009304: Fish skin cells got an immune-sentry role. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Ingerslev's team showed rainbow-trout fibroblasts act as immune sentinels during tissue damage. The PAMP/DAMP responses were mapped. The role feeds comparative immunology.
plos-pone-0011404: The RB1 pathway is one of the cell's main brakes on runaway division, and cancers often disable it. This research paper shows that a protein called RB1CC1 switches the pathway back on, slowing cancer cell growth and their ability to form colonies. Reactivating a built-in brake instead of adding a new drug points to a treatment strategy that works with the cell's own defenses.
plos-pone-0011504: Neuroticism — the tendency toward worry and emotional volatility — runs in families, but its genes were elusive. This genome-wide association study scans a population sample for DNA variants linked to the trait. The hunt adds hard genetic data to one of psychology's most studied personality dimensions.
plos-pone-0011604: Roseobacter bacteria teem in the oceans and help steer marine chemistry. This research paper rebuilds their family tree from whole genomes, tracing how the clan diversified. The tree shows these sea germs splitting into new roles that shape ocean life, from coastal waters to the open sea.
plos-pone-0011704: A mosquito's spit is more than an itch — it rewires immunity. This research paper shows Aedes aegypti saliva changes white blood cell recruitment and cytokine signals during West Nile virus infection. The saliva effect reveals the bite itself shapes the disease.
plos-pone-0011804: Inherited deafness can stem from hundreds of different gene glitches. This research paper puts a 198-mutation screening chip to the test, judging its worth in real clinics. The verdict tells doctors whether the chip earns a place in everyday care.
plos-pone-0011904: Tetherin is a primate protein that traps budding viruses — and viruses fight back. This research paper traces tetherin's molecular evolution across primates. The evolutionary arms race reveals how host defenses and viruses have shaped each other over millions of years.
plos-pone-0012004: Feline immunodeficiency virus plagues cats — and its US family tree was murky. This research paper performs a detailed phylogenetic analysis of FIV in the United States. The viral genealogy reveals how the cat virus spread and diversified across the country.
plos-pone-0012104: Malaria drugs must reach rural children fast — but do they? This prospective community study in rural Kilosa, Tanzania asks who gets prompt access to artemisinin-based combination therapy. The access audit reveals the gaps between policy and village reality today.
plos-pone-0012204: Childhood allergy blood markers mapped. This research paper studies relationships between serum IgE, cell-bound IgE, and IgE receptors on peripheral blood cells in a pediatric population. griffith-thompson-demotic-magical-papyru:
F. Ll. Griffith and Herbert Thompson published their edition of the great Demotic magical papyrus in 1904. The papyrus, split between London and Leiden collections, comes from Roman-era Egypt. Demotic script had kept its contents closed to most scholars.

Volume one gives full transliteration and English translation of the handbook. Spells address healing, protection, love, and speaking directly with gods. The editors' notes untangle the strange mixture of Egyptian, Greek, and Jewish elements. Their work remains the foundation for studying Egyptian magic of this period. Any serious reader of ancient spells still starts here.
reitzenstein-poimandres-1904:
Richard Reitzenstein published his study of the Poimandres in German in 1904. The Poimandres is the opening revelation of the Corpus Hermeticum, where Hermes receives a vision. Reitzenstein set that text inside its Graeco-Egyptian religious world.

He traced kinship between Hermetic writings, early Christianity, and Gnosticism. His method, the history-of-religions approach, treated texts as products of mixed cultures. The book founded a modern historical way of studying ancient mysticism. Scholars argued with his conclusions for decades, which proves his influence. Written for specialists, it changed how a whole field asked its questions.
audollent-defixionum-tabellae-1904:
Auguste Audollent published his corpus of ancient curse tablets in 1904. Ordinary Greeks and Romans scratched curses on lead and buried them in graves. Audollent collected every Greek and Latin example then known.

Binding spells target courtroom opponents, rival lovers, thieves, and athletes. Commentary explains each tablet's find spot, wording, and strange divine names. The corpus founded serious study of ancient magic's darker side. Later finds have added many tablets to Audollent's total. His collection remains the essential starting point for defixiones. The tablets preserve the grudges and fears of ordinary ancient people vividly.
letter-of-aristeas-thackeray-1904:
H. St. J. Thackeray translated the Letter of Aristeas into English in 1904. The Letter is a Hellenistic Jewish work about the making of the Septuagint. It purports to be a courtier's report to his brother.

The tale claims seventy-two scholars translated the Torah in seventy-two days. King Ptolemy's library in Alexandria supposedly commissioned the Greek Bible. Banquets, sage answers, and a tour of Jerusalem fill out the story. Scholars treat the account as charming legend rather than plain history. Its influence on later tradition was enormous regardless. Thackeray's translation presents the founding story of the Greek Bible gracefully.
